addedLines: - claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`; (5) `claude plugin eval` (writing and running plugin eval suites, its JSON/report, sandbox, CI, early-access enablement) and the `/skill-doctor` report. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- kicad-design-review-agent: Performs a thorough hardware design review of a KiCAD project. Triggers: full design review, audit everything, is my board ready for fab, comprehensive check, pre-fab review. (Tools: mcp__konnect__*)

- kicad-schematic-build-agent: Builds complete circuits from requirements or reference designs. Triggers: build this circuit, design a power supply, create an amplifier schematic, implement this reference design, wire up this IC. (Tools: mcp__konnect__*)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

## claude.ai Figma
The official Figma MCP server. Use this server whenever the user wants to create, generate, edit, implement, or sync any design, UI, screen, component, mockup, or visual — in Figma, FigJam, Figma Make, or Figma Slides — and whenever the user mentions Figma or provides a figma.com URL.

This server bridges code and design in both directions, and supports designing from scratch using existing design systems and codebases.

CAPABILITIES:
- Read designs FROM Figma into code (get_design_context, get_screenshot, get_metadata, get_figjam)
- Write designs INTO Figma from code, intent, or existing components (use_figma, generate_figma_design, create_new_file, upload_assets)
- Bridge code and design via Code Connect (get_code_connect_map, add_code_connect_map)
- Create diagrams and FigJam content (generate_diagram, get_figjam)

WHEN TO USE THESE TOOLS:
- The user wants to create, mock up, or generate any UI, screen, component, or design — even if Figma isn't named
- The user wants to implement a design as code (design-to-code)
- The user wants to push a page, view, or component into Figma (code-to-design)
- The user wants to update, sync, or edit an existing Figma file
- The user shares a figma.com URL
- The user wants to build or extend a design system, design tokens, or component library
- The user wants to create a diagram in FigJam

SKILLS (Prefer the skills shipped with the Figma plugin on the agent being used. If no Figma plugin is installed, use the skills served by the Figma MCP resource):
- /figma-use — MANDATORY before calling use_figma; fallback: skill://figma/figma-use/SKILL.md
- /figma-generate-design — for translating an app page or layout into Figma; fallback: skill://figma/figma-generate-design/SKILL.md
- /figma-generate-library — for building a design system in Figma from code; fallback: skill://figma/figma-generate-library/SKILL.md
- /figma-code-connect — for mapping Figma components to codebase components; fallback: skill://figma/figma-code-connect/SKILL.md
- /figma-use-figjam — for FigJam-specific use_f… [truncated]

## claude.ai Semrush
Semrush MCP provides SEO, traffic, and competitive intelligence data.

IMPORTANT: Always call tools to fetch real Semrush data. Do not answer from general knowledge when data can be retrieved. Do not ask the user for parameters you can infer — just call the tool.

Workflow: discovery tool → get_report_schema → execute_report. For complex tasks, call execute_report multiple times with different parameters or combine reports from multiple toolkits if needed.
  Default "database" to "us" when not specified. Use display_limit=30-50 for exploratory queries.

## pencil
The Pencil MCP server is the editor for .pen design files (web/mobile apps and websites). Use it to read, generate, and validate designs.

.pen files are encrypted: access them only via "pencil" MCP tools — never use Read or Grep on .pen files. Follow each tool's input schema exactly.

Always call get_editor_state(include_schema: true) if you don't have the current .pen file schema in the context. Knowing the schema is required to use any other Pencil MCP tool.

Tools: get_editor_state, get_guidelines, batch_get, batch_design, snapshot_layout, get_screenshot, get_variables, set_variables, export_nodes.

- agents-sdk: Build AI agents on Cloudflare Workers using the Agents SDK. Load when creating stateful agents, durable workflows, real-time WebSocket apps, scheduled tasks, MCP servers, chat applications, voice agents, or browser automation. Covers Agent class, state management, callable RPC, Workflows, durable execution, queues, retries, observability, and React hooks. Biases towards retrieval from Cloudflare docs over pre-trained knowledge.
- cloudflare: Comprehensive Cloudflare platform skill covering Workers, Pages, storage (KV, D1, R2), AI (Workers AI, Vectorize, Agents SDK), feature flags (Flagship), networking (Tunnel, Spectrum), security (WAF, DDoS), and infrastructure-as-code (Terraform, Pulumi). Use for any Cloudflare development task. Biases towards retrieval from Cloudflare docs over pre-trained knowledge.
- cloudflare-email-service: Send and receive transactional emails with Cloudflare Email Service (Email Sending + Email Routing). Use when building email sending (Workers binding or REST API), email routing, Agents SDK email handling, or integrating email into any app — Workers, Node.js, Python, Go, etc. Also use for email deliverability, SPF/DKIM/DMARC, wrangler email setup, MCP email tools, or when a coding agent needs to send emails. Even for simple requests like "add email to my Worker" — this skill has critical config details.
- durable-objects: Create and review Cloudflare Durable Objects. Use when building stateful coordination (chat rooms, multiplayer games, booking systems), implementing RPC methods, SQLite storage, alarms, WebSockets, or reviewing DO code for best practices. Covers Workers integration, wrangler config, and testing with Vitest. Biases towards retrieval from Cloudflare docs over pre-trained knowledge.
- impeccable: Use when the user wants to design, redesign, shape, critique, audit, polish, clarify, distill, harden, optimize, adapt, animate, colorize, extract, or otherwise improve a frontend interface. Covers websites, landing pages, dashboards, product UI, app shells, components, forms, settings, onboarding, and empty states. Handles UX review, visual hierarchy, information architecture, cognitive load, accessibility, performance, responsive behavior, theming, anti-patterns, typography, fonts, spacing, layout, alignment, color, motion, micro-interactions, UX copy, error states, edge cases, i18n, and reusable design systems or tokens. Also use for bland designs that need to become bolder or more delightful, loud designs that should become quieter, live browser iteration on UI elements, or ambitious visual effects that should feel technically extraordinary. Not for backend-only or non-UI tasks.
- kicad-library: Library management workflow for KiCAD — creating symbols, footprints, and managing libraries
via MCP tools. Triggers on: "create a symbol", "make a footprint", "custom component",
"register library", "find a part", "pin numbering", "new symbol", "new footprint",
"add to library", "library path", "pad layout".
- kicad-manufacture: Manufacturing and fabrication workflow for KiCAD projects via MCP tools. Triggers on: "send to fab",
"order boards", "gerbers", "JLCPCB", "manufacturing", "export for production", "pick and place",
"assembly files", "generate fabrication outputs", "BOM for fab", "production files", "fab house".
- kicad-pcb: Workflow skill for KiCAD PCB layout and routing via MCP tools. Triggers on: "layout the board",
"route traces", "PCB", "place footprints", "copper pour", "board outline", "differential pair",
"board setup", "track width", "via", "zone", "design rules", "stackup", "silkscreen".
- kicad-review: Design review and validation workflow for KiCAD projects via MCP tools. Triggers on: "review my design",
"check for errors", "audit", "DRC", "ERC", "find problems", "design review", "is this ready",
"validate", "check my schematic", "check my PCB", "what's wrong", "run checks", "pre-fab review".
- kicad-schematic: Workflow skill for KiCAD schematic design via MCP tools. Triggers on: "design a circuit",
"add a component", "wire up", "connect pins", "build schematic", "place resistor",
"place cap", "place IC", "schematic", "add symbol", "net label", "power rail".
- konnect: Mandatory operating rules for ANY task involving KiCAD projects. Loaded when the user mentions KiCAD, schematics, PCBs, or any .kicad_* file. Prevents file corruption by routing all changes through Konnect MCP tools.
- sandbox-sdk: Build sandboxed applications for secure code execution. Load when building AI code execution, code interpreters, CI/CD systems, interactive dev environments, or executing untrusted code. Covers Sandbox SDK lifecycle, commands, files, code interpreter, and preview URLs. Biases towards retrieval from Cloudflare docs over pre-trained knowledge.
- web-perf: Analyzes web performance using Chrome DevTools MCP. Measures Core Web Vitals (LCP, INP, CLS) and supplementary metrics (FCP, TBT, Speed Index), identifies render-blocking resources, network dependency chains, layout shifts, caching issues, and accessibility gaps. Use when asked to audit, profile, debug, or optimize page load performance, Lighthouse scores, or site speed. Biases towards retrieval from current documentation over pre-trained knowledge.
- workers-best-practices: Reviews and authors Cloudflare Workers code against production best practices. Load when writing new Workers, reviewing Worker code, configuring wrangler.jsonc, or checking for common Workers anti-patterns (streaming, floating promises, global state, secrets, bindings, observability). Biases towards retrieval from Cloudflare docs over pre-trained knowledge.
- wrangler: Cloudflare Workers CLI for deploying, developing, and managing Workers, KV, R2, D1, Vectorize, Hyperdrive, Workers AI, Containers, Queues, Workflows, Pipelines, and Secrets Store. Load before running wrangler commands to ensure correct syntax and best practices. Biases towards retrieval from Cloudflare docs over pre-trained knowledge.
- tested-code-review: Adversarial code review where every finding is proven by an executed test/repro and verified by an adversarial review panel - When the user wants a comprehensive, test-backed review of a branch/diff: findings must be demonstrated with real executed tests (locally and/or on provided ssh test hosts) plus reachability justification, then survive adversarial reviewers. Args: { repo?, branch?, base?, remotes?: [ssh strings], instructions?, effort?: low|medium|high|max }.
- frontend-design:frontend-design: Guidance for distinctive, intentional visual design when building new UI or reshaping an existing one. Helps with aesthetic direction, typography, and making choices that don't read as templated defaults.
- paper-desktop:code-to-design: Generate a Paper design from the project's codebase — using its tokens, styles, and components as context.
- paper-desktop:design-to-code: Turn a Paper design into production code using the project's existing conventions.
- design: Create a design canvas — a multi-artboard visual design published as an Artifact that runs Claude Design's canvas editor (an early preview of Claude Design inside Claude Code). You DRAFT the design as .dc.html artboards laid out on one pan/zoom canvas; where saving is enabled for the user's account they refine every element visually (click-to-select, a properties panel, inline text editing, undo/redo) and Save publishes a new version for everyone, otherwise they get a view-and-export (PNG/PDF) preview of your draft. Good for UI mockups and screen flows, landing pages, marketing and social graphics, and print pieces — posters, flyers, brochures as single-page artboards; memos and reports as one flowing artboard. Use when someone wants a design, mockup, wireframe, UI or screen design, landing page, poster, flyer, brochure, banner, card, one-pager, or any visual layout they would rather tweak by hand than in code. Only for CREATING or re-seeding a canvas; an existing one is edited in its published Artifact.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including a skill-instructed Markdown one — Markdown is never a shortcut past the design pass.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts — when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, remembering what people do on it (a poll, a sign-up sheet, a checklist, a document edited in place — it saves new versions of itself), keeping state shared across viewers, knowing who is viewing, asking Claude a question of its own, storing files people add, or handing the viewer a file to save. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).

8. Check infra/ for wrangler/alchemy config: smart placement, compatibility date, observability, any limits.

# The action consumers wire into their CI: install Determinate Nix trusting
# this cache, provision the job's read credential before the daemon starts,
# download the pinned cachet binary, and hand the push phases to the nested
# main/post action. Signing happens server-side, so the action holds no key
# material; the job's OIDC token is the only credential it ever touches.
name: cachet setup
description: >-
  Install Determinate Nix wired to a cachet deployment, then push what the
  job builds. Grant `permissions: { contents: read, id-token: write }` for
  the full path; in a job whose context cannot receive the grant (a forked
  pull request) the action installs plain nix and the build runs uncached,
  slower and green. Network failures inside the action degrade the same
  way: never a red job over a blip.
author: nox-systems
inputs:
  cache-url:
    description: The cache's base URL.
    required: true
  roots:
    description: >-
      Flake installables whose closures this project keeps. Their outputs
      are pushed unconditionally and, on the default branch, become the
      project's garbage-collection lease.
    required: false
    default: ""
  audience:
    description: The OIDC audience the cache requires.
    required: false
    default: cachet
  project:
    description: >-
      The lease name for this repository. Defaults to the owner and name
      joined by a hyphen (`my-org-my-repo`), because a renewal replaces the
      lease wholesale: two same-named repositories in one org would
      otherwise overwrite each other's.
    required: false
    default: ""

    description: >-

      cache: cachet stores what the job pushes. Kept declared so existing

    required: false

      The ref permitted to renew the lease. The cache enforces this itself;
      this input only avoids a request that would be refused.
    required: false

content.content:
# no token plumbing for forked pull requests — by design, so that
        # arbitrary code cannot impersonate the repo. The right answer
        # there is a plain build: skip every cache-related write so the
        # job continues uncached instead of dying before nix exists.
        if [ -z "${ACTIONS_ID_TOKEN_REQUEST_URL:-}" ]; then
          echo "cachet: no OIDC token grant in this job (a forked pull request, or missing id-token: write)."
          echo "  nix installs and builds WITHOUT the ${CACHET_CACHE_URL} cache; everything else runs normally."
          echo "  Forks that want caching: deploy cachet and point cache-url at it."
          echo "CACHET_EXTRA_CONF=" >> "${GITHUB_ENV}"
          exit 0
        fi
        # A token fetch that dies on the network is the same class as a
        # fork: setup could not complete, the build continues uncached.
        # --retry covers the blips (connection resets, DNS, 5xx), and what
        # outlives them degrades as loud log lines with the job green.
        if ! token="$(curl -fsSL --retry 4 --retry-all-errors --retry-delay 2 \
          -H "Authorization: Bearer ${ACTIONS_ID_TOKEN_REQUEST_TOKEN}" \
          "${ACTIONS_ID_TOKEN_REQUEST_URL}&audience=${CACHET_AUDIENCE}" | jq -r '.value')"; then
          echo "cachet: the OIDC token fetch failed on the network after retries."
          echo "  nix installs and builds WITHOUT the ${CACHET_CACHE_URL} cache; everything else runs normally."
          echo "CACHET_EXTRA_CONF=" >> "${GITHUB_ENV}"
          exit 0
        fi
        host="$(printf '%s' "${CACHET_CACHE_URL}" | sed -e 's#^https\?://##' -e 's#/.*$##')"

        # The credential file: real, outside the nix store, 0600.
        sudo mkdir -p /etc/nix /etc/determinate
        printf 'machine %s login cachet password %s\n' "${host}" "${token}" \
          | sudo tee /etc/nix/netrc >/dev/null
        sudo chmod 600 /etc/nix/netrc

        # Register it under authentication.additionalNetrcSources, merging
        # when the installer pre-seeded the file.
        if [ -f /etc/determinate/config.json ]; then
          sudo cat /etc/determinate/config.json \
            | jq '.authentication.additionalNetrcSources = ((.authentication.additionalNetrcSources // []) + ["/etc/nix/netrc"] | unique)' \
            | sudo tee /etc/determinate/config.json.tmp >/dev/null
          sudo mv /etc/determinate/config.json.tmp /etc/determinate/config.json
        else
          printf '{"authentication":{"additionalNetrcSources":["/etc/nix/netrc"]}}\n' \
            | sudo tee /etc/determinate/config.json >/dev/null
        fi

        # The deployment names its own signing key: fetch the public half
        # from the worker rather than asking consumers to paste it. This
        # doubles as the connectivity check: a cache that cannot answer its
        # public config fails the job here, before the build starts. The
        # retry only asks that "cannot answer" outlive a blip.
        public_key="$(curl -fsSL --retry 4 --retry-all-errors --retry-delay 2 "${CACHET_CACHE_URL%/}/api/public/config" | jq -r '.publicKey')"
        # why: nix treats the key settings as restricted, so an untrusted
        # caller's extra-trusted-public-keys line is parsed and dropped;
        # the invoking user must itself be trusted for the key to count.
        {
          echo "CACHET_EXTRA_CONF<<EOF_CACHET_CONF"
          echo "extra-substituters = ${CACHET_CACHE_URL%/}"
          echo "extra-trusted-public-keys = ${public_key}"
          echo "trusted-users = root $(whoami)"
          echo "EOF_CACHET_CONF"
        } >> "${GITHUB_ENV}"
        echo "cachet: read credential provisioned before Determinate starts"

    - uses: DeterminateSystems/determinate-nix-action@61cbfe2efc2d4e7a8a6d56967c3c1058e846c858 # v3.21.9
      with:
        # The substituter and trusted key ride the install because a
        # substituter added after the daemon has started is never consulted.
        # In a job with no OIDC grant the provisioning step answered empty,
        # and this install answers plain upstream-only nix.
        extra-conf: ${{ env.CACHET_EXTRA_CONF }}

    # The Determinate installer logged into FlakeHub on this runner (any job
    # granting id-token: write gets one), which adds cache.flakehub.com as a
    # substituter: every lookup then pays a 401 round trip before falling
    # through to cachet. Log out; the cachet credential is independent.
    - name: Log out of FlakeHub Cache, which this deployment does not use
      shell: bash
      run: |
        set -euo pipefail
        # `|| true`: a job without id-token never logged in, so logout is a
        # no-op there, and this action must not fail a build over a cache it
        # does not use.
        sudo determinate-nixd auth logout || true
        sudo determinate-nixd status || true

    - name: Download and verify the cachet binary
      shell: bash
      env:
        CACHET_VERSION: ${{ inputs.cachet-version }}
      run: |
        set -euo pipefail
        case "${{ runner.os }}-${{ runner.arch }}" in
          Linux-X64) triple="x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu" ;;
          Linux-ARM64) triple="aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu" ;;
          macOS-X64) triple="x86_64-apple-darwin" ;;
          macOS-ARM64) triple="aarch64-apple-darwin" ;;
          *)
            echo "cachet: no cachet release for ${{ runner.os }}-${{ runner.arch }}" >&2
            exit 1
            ;;
        esac
        base="https://github.com/nox-systems/cachet/releases/download/v${CACHET_VERSION}"
        # cargo-dist names archives after the package, not the binary.
        artifact="cachet-cli-${triple}.tar.xz"
        work="$(mktemp -d)"
        # A download that dies on the network must not red the job:
        # --retry sweeps up the blips (the releases CDN resets
        # connections), and a persistent outage downgrades this job to
        # read-only, because push is an optimization the build owes
        # nobody. The nested action prints its own degrade line when
        # CACHET_BIN stays unset.
        if curl -fsSL --retry 4 --retry-all-errors --retry-delay 2 \
             -o "${work}/${artifact}" "${base}/${artifact}" \
          && curl -fsSL --retry 4 --retry-all-errors --retry-delay 2 \
            -o "${work}/${artifact}.sha256" "${base}/${artifact}.sha256"; then
          # The checksum verifies before the archive opens: a tampered or
          # truncated download fails the job, it does not limp onward.
          # Blank lines dropped first: cargo-dist's checksum files end in
          # an empty line, which shasum warns on as unformatted while the
          # real line checks fine. The warning is noise the job log does
          # not need.
          (cd "${work}" && grep -v '^[[:space:]]*$' "${artifact}.sha256" | shasum -a 256 -c -)
          install_dir="${RUNNER_TEMP}/cachet-bin"
          mkdir -p "${install_dir}"
          tar -xJf "${work}/${artifact}" -C "${install_dir}" --strip-components=1
          rm -rf "${work}"
          echo "CACHET_BIN=${install_dir}/cachet" >> "${GITHUB_ENV}"
          "${install_dir}/cachet" --version
        else
          rm -rf "${work}"
          echo "cachet: the release download failed on the network after retries."
          echo "  nix and the build continue; this job will not push."
        fi

    - name: Configure cachet
      shell: bash
      env:
        CACHET_CACHE_URL: ${{ inputs.cache-url }}
        CACHET_AUDIENCE: ${{ inputs.audience }}
        CACHET_PROJECT: ${{ inputs.project }}
        CACHET_ROOTS: ${{ inputs.roots }}
        CACHET_DEFAULT_BRANCH_REF: ${{ inputs.default-branch-ref }}
        CACHET_PUSH: ${{ inputs.push }}
      run: |
        set -euo pipefail

        # Confirm the daemon's netrc authenticates against cachet, so a
        # regression surfaces in the log rather than as a silent rebuild: a
        # 404 means the credential is present and authenticated (the probed
        # path is simply absent), while a 401 means it is not.
        daemon_netrc="$(nix config show netrc-file 2>/dev/null || echo /nix/var/determinate/netrc)"
        probe_code="$(curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' --netrc-file "${daemon_netrc}" \
          "${CACHET_CACHE_URL%/}/0000000000000000000000000000000a.narinfo" 2>/dev/null || echo 000)"
        echo "cachet: read auth probe returned ${probe_code} (404 = authenticated, 401 = not)"

        # Everything the post step reads is exported here, and this is the
        # only place any of it is resolved. A step-level `env:` block is
        # scoped to its own step, so passing these to the nested action as
        # `with:` inputs left the post step reading empty strings.
        project="${CACHET_PROJECT}"
        if [ -z "${project}" ]; then
          project="${GITHUB_REPOSITORY//\//-}"
        fi
        # why: the heredoc form rather than `NAME=value`. `roots` takes
        # several installables and the post step splits on any whitespace,
        # so a caller writing them one per line with a YAML block scalar is
        # using the documented shape, and a bare `NAME=value` line cannot
        # express a newline: GitHub rejects the whole file with "Invalid
        # format" when it sees the continuation.
        env_file() {
          printf '%s<<CACHET_EOF_1c7f\n%s\nCACHET_EOF_1c7f\n' "$1" "$2" >> "${GITHUB_ENV}"
        }
        env_file CACHET_CACHE_URL "${CACHET_CACHE_URL%/}"
        env_file CACHET_AUDIENCE "${CACHET_AUDIENCE}"
        env_file CACHET_PROJECT "${project}"
        env_file CACHET_ROOTS "${CACHET_ROOTS}"
        env_file CACHET_DEFAULT_BRANCH_REF "${CACHET_DEFAULT_BRANCH_REF}"
        env_file CACHET_PUSH "${CACHET_PUSH}"
        echo "cachet: configured ${CACHET_CACHE_URL} as a substituter for project ${project}"

    # The nested JavaScript action: its main step snapshots the store, and
    # its post step, on success only, pushes. It reads no inputs, because
    # the step above resolved everything into the job environment.
    # why: the full owner/repo/path@ref form rather than `./post`. A
    # composite action resolves a relative `./post` against the consumer's
    # workspace rather than this action's own directory, so a cross-repo
    # consumer failed with "Can't find 'action.yml'". The ref names the v1
    # major tag, which every release in the 1.x line moves forward, so the
    # composite and its post action always come from the same line.
    - uses: nox-systems/cachet/action/post@v0

        project="${CACHET_PROJECT}"
        if [ -z "${project}" ]; then
          project="${GITHUB_REPOSITORY//\//-}"
        fi
        # why: the heredoc form rather than `NAME=value`. `roots` takes
        # several installables and the post step splits on any whitespace,
        # so a caller writing them one per line with a YAML block scalar is
        # using the documented shape, and a bare `NAME=value` line cannot
        # express a newline: GitHub rejects the whole file with "Invalid
        # format" when it sees the continuation.
        env_file() {
          printf '%s<<CACHET_EOF_1c7f\n%s\nCACHET_EOF_1c7f\n' "$1" "$2" >> "${GITHUB_ENV}"
        }
        env_file CACHET_CACHE_URL "${CACHET_CACHE_URL%/}"
        env_file CACHET_AUDIENCE "${CACHET_AUDIENCE}"
        env_file CACHET_PROJECT "${project}"
        env_file CACHET_ROOTS "${CACHET_ROOTS}"
        env_file CACHET_DEFAULT_BRANCH_REF "${CACHET_DEFAULT_BRANCH_REF}"
        env_file CACHET_PUSH "${CACHET_PUSH}"
        echo "cachet: configured ${CACHET_CACHE_URL} as a substituter for project ${project}"

    # The nested JavaScript action: its main step snapshots the store, and
    # its post step, on success only, pushes. It reads no inputs, because
    # the step above resolved everything into the job environment.
    # why: the full owner/repo/path@ref form rather than `./post`. A
    # composite action resolves a relative `./post` against the consumer's
    # workspace rather than this action's own directory, so a cross-repo
    # consumer failed with "Can't find 'action.yml'". The ref names the v1
    # major tag, which every release in the 1.x line moves forward, so the
    # composite and its post action always come from the same line.
    - uses: nox-systems/cachet/action/post@v0

<result>## Bottom line first

The old TypeScript client has **no upload concurrency at all** — store paths are uploaded one at a time, and multipart parts are uploaded one at a time, strictly sequentially. Its speed did not come from parallelism in the uploader. It came from four things:

1. **It almost never uploads anything.** Two filter stages (16-way concurrent HEAD probes) delete the work before it exists.
2. **All the expensive byte work is done by `nix copy` itself**, in one native invocation, not in JS. No zstd library, no `zstd` subprocess, no NAR serialization in the client.
3. **The Worker does essentially nothing per write** — one `head()` for narinfos, a straight stream into R2 for NARs. No hashing, no decompression, no signature verification.
4. **The read path is Cache-API-first with 30-day immutable TTLs**, so nearly every read is a PoP hit and never touches R2 or the Worker's logic beyond one SHA-256 comparison.

---

## 1. UPLOAD PATH

### 1a. Store-path concurrency: **1 (sequential)** — and there is no constant or env var for it

`/Users/shivanshvij/Development/cachet/action/post/src/post.ts:78-90`:

```ts
let uploaded = 0;
for (const object of uploadOrder(files.value)) {
    const plan = planUpload(object);
    if (!plan.ok) { return plan; }
    const sent = await uploadObject(target, plan.value);   // ← awaited in-loop
    if (!sent.ok) { return sent; }
    uploaded += 1;
}
```

The **only** bounded-concurrency primitive in the whole client is `mapWithConcurrency` at `/Users/shivanshvij/Development/cachet/action/post/src/core/filter.ts:56-79`, and it is used **exclusively for the two HEAD-probe filter stages**, never for uploads:

- `filter.ts:103` — `mapWithConcurrency(probeable, FILTER_CONCURRENCY_MAX, …)` (upstream probes)
- `filter.ts:164` — `mapWithConcurrency(candidates, FILTER_CONCURRENCY_MAX, …)` (cachet probes)

The constant, `/Users/shivanshvij/Development/cachet/src/core/constants.ts:224`:

```ts
export const FILTER_CONCURRENCY_MAX = 16;
```

### 1b. Parts per object concurrency: **1 (sequential)**

`/Users/shivanshvij/Development/cachet/action/post/src/real/upload.ts:193-200`:

```ts
for (let partNumber = 1; partNumber <= plan.expectedParts; partNumber += 1) {
    const sent = await uploadOnePart(target, plan, uploadId, partNumber, bytes.value);
    if (!sent.ok) {
        await abortUpload(target, plan, uploadId);
        return sent;
    }
    parts.push(sent.value);
}
return completeUpload(target, plan, uploadId, parts);
```

Note also `upload.ts:182` — the *entire object* is read into a Node `Buffer` before any part is sent (`readStagedFile`, `/Users/shivanshvij/Development/cachet/action/post/src/real/host.ts:105-112`), and each part is a `bytes.subarray()` slice (`upload.ts:110`). Fully buffered, not streamed. That was acceptable only because multipart is nearly never hit — ADR 0002 says so explicitly: *"the multipart wrappers … are rarely exercised in production, because the upstream filter keeps the fat NARs that would need them out of the bucket almost entirely."*

### 1c. Compression: **zstd, done by Nix, not by the client**

`/Users/shivanshvij/Development/cachet/action/post/src/post.ts:63-66`:

```ts
const stagingRoot = await mkdtemp(join(tmpdir(), 'cachet-staging-'));
const destination = `file://${stagingRoot}?compression=zstd&secret-key=${inputs.signingKeyFile}`;
const staged = await run(['nix', 'copy', '--to', destination, ...paths]);
```

- **Which zstd:** Nix's own linked libzstd, invoked through the `file://` store's `compression=zstd` URL parameter.
- **Level:** unset → Nix's default (`compression-level` is never passed anywhere in the repo; I grepped for it and it does not appear).
- **Streaming or buffered:** Nix streams internally; the *client* then buffers the finished `.nar.zst` file off disk. There is no streaming anywhere in the JS uploader.
- **Library vs. binary:** **neither.** `package.json` has exactly two runtime deps — `hono` and `jose`. No zstd anything. The client never sees an uncompressed NAR; it never calls `nix dump-path`.
- **Signing happens in the same call**, via `secret-key=` — one native pass does NAR serialization + zstd + Ed25519 signing + narinfo emission for the entire closure.

Critically: this is **one `nix copy` invocation for the whole path set**, so Nix's internal copy thread pool (`max-substitution-jobs`, default 16) parallelizes serialization/compression/signing across paths natively. The JS side only moves already-finished files.

Documented at `/Users/shivanshvij/Development/cachet/docs/design/action.md:76-78` and `/Users/shivanshvij/Development/cachet/docs/adr/0004-client-side-signing.md` §Decision 1.

### 1d. Multipart part size and thresholds

`/Users/shivanshvij/Development/cachet/src/core/constants.ts`:

| Constant | Line | Value |
|---|---|---|
| `UPLOAD_SINGLE_MAX_BYTES` | 159 | `94_371_840` (90 MiB) — single-PUT cutoff |
| `UPLOAD_PART_BYTES` | 166 | `67_108_864` (**64 MiB**) — every part but the last, exactly |
| `R2_PART_MIN_BYTES` | 169 | `5_242_880` |
| `MULTIPART_PARTS_MAX` | 176 | `1_000` (≈64 GiB ceiling) |
| `UPLOAD_RETRY_MAX` | 192 | `3` |
| `UPLOAD_RETRY_BASE_DELAY_MS` | ~207 | `500`, linear backoff |

The part plan is computed by the **Worker's own** `planParts` imported into the client (`/Users/shivanshvij/Development/cachet/action/post/src/core/upload-plan.ts:18-19, 70`), so client and server cannot disagree. `planParts` is at `/Users/shivanshvij/Development/cachet/src/core/routes/multipart.ts:58-77`.

### 1e. Presigned URLs / direct-to-R2: **No. Everything goes through the Worker.**

This is an explicit, argued architectural commitment, not an oversight — `/Users/shivanshvij/Development/cachet/docs/adr/0002-writes-through-the-worker.md`, Alternatives considered:

> **Presigned URLs issued by the Worker.** Rejected: a presigned URL bypasses the Worker… It trades an enforceable invariant for a URL-construction bug class, and it is on the OUT list for that reason.

> **A presigned direct upload followed by a Worker "commit" call.** Rejected…

There is no R2 access key anywhere in the system. Routes: `PUT /{hash}.narinfo`, `PUT /nar/*`, `POST /nar/*?uploads`, `PUT /nar/*?uploadId&partNumber`, `POST /nar/*?uploadId`, `DELETE /nar/*?uploadId` (`/Users/shivanshvij/Development/cachet/src/worker.ts:70-172`).

### 1f. Does it stream `nix dump-path` into an HTTP body? **No.**

The pipeline is: `nix copy --to file://$TMPDIR` → walk the staging dir (`host.ts:56-89`) → `readFile()` the whole object into a Buffer → `fetch(PUT, body: new Uint8Array(bytes))` (`upload.ts:57, 70`). Disk round-trip, full buffering.

### 1g. ⭐ The actual reason uploads were fast: the double filter

`/Users/shivanshvij/Development/cachet/action/post/src/post.ts:104-134`:

1. **`filterAgainstUpstream`** — 16-way concurrent `HEAD https://cache.nixos.org/{hash}.narinfo`. Hit ⇒ drop the path. (`filter.ts:88-131`, probe at `host.ts:157-180`.)
2. **`dropAlreadyCached`** — 16-way concurrent `HEAD https://pkg-cache…/{hash}.narinfo` with the job's own OIDC bearer. Hit ⇒ drop. (`filter.ts:150-190`, probe at `host.ts:182-207`.)
3. Only what survives both is passed to `nix copy` — so **nothing is compressed, staged, or written to disk for a path the cache already has.**

Git commit `04d5e38 action: skip staging and uploading paths cachet already holds` added step 2. Its docstring (`filter.ts:133-148`) is the key sentence:

> `nix copy` would have skipped them, because it checks presence at the destination; staging to a local `file://` first throws that check away, so this restores it by asking cachet directly **before a single byte is compressed or sent**.

Steady state on a warm cache: `toUpload.length === 0`, `post.ts` returns at line 129 without ever invoking `nix copy`. The sequential upload loop costs nothing because it iterates over an empty set.

Also: a fresh OIDC token is minted per request (`upload.ts:26-32`) — a local call to the runner's token endpoint, milliseconds — to avoid `ERR_JWT_EXPIRED` on the narinfos that go last.

---

## 2. DOWNLOAD / READ PATH

All in `/Users/shivanshvij/Development/cachet/src/real/read-handlers.ts:110-158`.

**Order:** resolve generation (edge cache) → `cache.match(objectCacheKey)` → R2 `get()` → stream through.

```ts
// read-handlers.ts:145-147
const response = new Response(object.body, {
    headers: objectResponseHeaders(kind, object.size),
});
```

- **R2 body streamed straight through, never buffered** — `object.body` is handed directly to `Response`. Justified against the 128 MB isolate limit (`docs/contracts.md:142`).
- **Cache API: yes, aggressively.** `caches.default`, keys composed under a synthetic origin so they're independent of the request hostname:
  - `objectCacheKey` — `/Users/shivanshvij/Development/cachet/src/core/routes/generation.ts:97-100`: `https://cachet-edge.invalid/g{N}{path}`
  - `EDGE_CACHE_KEY_ORIGIN` — `constants.ts:404`
- **TTLs** (`/Users/shivanshvij/Development/cachet/src/core/routes/read.ts:41-52` + constants):
  - narinfo: `2_592_000` s (30 days), `public, max-age=…, immutable` (`constants.ts:234`)
  - NAR: `2_592_000` s, same (`constants.ts:237`)
  - **404s are cached** at `30` s (`constants.ts:244`) — *"an uncached 404 costs an R2 round trip per query"* (`read.ts:54-60`). This is a real win: Nix HEADs/GETs a narinfo for every path in a closure, most of which the cache doesn't have.
  - `/nix-cache-info`: `300` s
  - generation doc: `60` s (`constants.ts:254`)
  - objects > `536_870_912` bytes (512 MB) stream uncached (`constants.ts:260`)
- **Cache writes never block the response** — `waitUntil(cache.put(...))` at `read-handlers.ts:81, 140, 153`.
- **Generation resolution costs one near-free `cache.match` per request**, one R2 GET per PoP per minute, not per request (`read-handlers.ts:47-88`, ADR 0012 §3).
- **No redirects, no presigned GETs, no public R2 bucket.** Same OUT-list commitment as writes.
- **HEAD is answered from `env.CACHE_BUCKET.head()` metadata only and is not edge-cached** (`read-handlers.ts:96-106`) — deliberate, since Nix uses GET for the queries that matter.
- **Read auth is cheap by design.** `/Users/shivanshvij/Development/cachet/src/core/auth/authorize.ts:117-130`: the credential (Bearer *or* netrc Basic password) is first compared as a SHA-256 hex digest against ≤2 configured slots — one hash, no network. Only a JWT-shaped value that misses both slots takes the RS256 path, and the JWKS is module-scope cached per isolate for `JWKS_CACHE_TTL_MS = 600_000` (`constants.ts:118`, cache at `/Users/shivanshvij/Development/cachet/src/real/request.ts:29`).

ADR 0012's framing (`docs/adr/0012-edge-cache-generation.md:12-33`) is the design's own performance statement:

> The read path exists to be fast. A `nix build` issues one narinfo request per store path in the closure… What makes that acceptable is Cloudflare's edge cache… A five-minute TTL on narinfos turns a warm closure resolution from a few hundred edge hits into a few hundred R2 GETs at every point of presence seeing traffic, forever, on the hottest path in the system.

---

## 3. WORKER: verify-then-sign on upload?

**Neither. There is no signing and no signature verification anywhere in the Worker.** Signing is 100% client-side, inside `nix copy --secret-key`.

- `/Users/shivanshvij/Development/cachet/docs/adr/0004-client-side-signing.md` §Decision 2: *"The signing key is never read by the Worker, the bucket, or the collector… The Worker has no signing primitive, no private key binding, and no route that would take one."*
- There is a **test gate** enforcing it: `test/fast/gate/no-signing-key.test.ts` — asserts no source file imports a private key or calls a signing primitive (`CLAUDE.md:79`, `docs/operations.md:83`).
- §Decision 6: the Worker's entire crypto surface is SHA-256 (read-token compare) + `jose` JWT verification.

What the Worker actually does per write (`/Users/shivanshvij/Development/cachet/src/real/write-handlers.ts`):

- **`PUT /nar/*` (`putNar`, lines 91-111):** Content-Length guard, then `env.CACHE_BUCKET.put(key, request.body)` — **the request body stream is handed straight to R2.** No hashing, no zstd decode, no NAR parse. Line 108: *"A repeated write is harmless: both kinds are content-addressed."*
- **`PUT /{hash}.narinfo` (`putNarinfo`, lines 52-89):** Content-Length ≤ 64 KiB, `request.text()`, parse, **one `env.CACHE_BUCKET.head()`** on the referenced NAR key (the NEVER-DANGLE check), then `put()` of the **exact received bytes** (line 84 — never re-serialized, because that would break the client's signature).
- **`uploadPart` (lines 175-207):** length guard, one R2 `get()` of the `uploads/{id}` bookkeeping record, size check, `resumeMultipartUpload().uploadPart(n, request.body)` — again a raw stream passthrough.

Nothing is deferred to `waitUntil` on the write path; there's simply almost nothing to defer. CPU budget is capped at 250 ms (see below).

---

## 4. Explicit performance notes / benchmarks / tuning knobs in docs

**There are no benchmark numbers anywhere in the repo.** I grepped for MB/s, timings, benchmark tables — nothing. What exists is reasoning:

- `/Users/shivanshvij/Development/cachet/CLAUDE.md:220` — *"Priority order, always: **Safety → Performance → Developer Experience.**"* (TigerStyle)

The old TypeScript client has **no upload concurrency at all** — store paths are uploaded one at a time, and multipart parts are uploaded one at a time, strictly sequentially. Its speed did not come from parallelism in the uploader. It came from four things:

## 1. CONCURRENCY

### Store paths in parallel: there is no per-path concurrency at all — the unit is the *object*, and objects go in **barrier'd waves of 16**

```rust

`UPLOAD_WAVE_BYTES` = 4 × 94,371,800 = **377,487,200 B (~360 MiB)** per wave.

The runner is `wave_run`, `pipeline.rs:346-365`. It is **not** `buffer_unordered` and **not** a semaphore — it is a hard barrier partition:

```rust
// crates/cachet-push/src/pipeline.rs:352-364
    let mut done = Vec::with_capacity(items.len());

Consequence: each wave costs `max(latency of its 16 members)`, not `avg`. One slow 90 MiB PUT stalls 15 finished slots. 1. `bucket.head(document.url.as_str())` — `write.rs:415` (R2 op #1 of the narinfo request).
2. `bucket.get(document.url.as_str()).execute()` — `write.rs:425-435` (**re-fetches the object the client just uploaded**).
3. `measure_nar(body, is_zst, document.nar_size_bytes)` — `write.rs:444` → `write.rs:568-641`. This streams the **entire** compressed object through:
   - `Sha256Stream` over the compressed bytes (`write.rs:573`, `write.rs:579`),
   - `ZstdStream` (pure-Rust `ruzstd`, `crates/cachet-crypto/src/zstd_stream.rs`) fed in ≤4 MiB slices (`FEED_MAX`, `write.rs:560`, loop at `write.rs:587-611`),

4. `VerifiedNar::verify` — `write.rs:450-456` (`crates/cachet-core/src/write.rs:91-122`).

**Verify-then-sign is fully inline and fully blocking on the upload request.** There is no queue, no Durable Object, no `ctx.waitUntil`, no deferral. | `PUT /<hash>.narinfo` | `head` (`write.rs:415`), `get` + full body stream (`write.rs:425`, `write.rs:576-615`), `put` narinfo (`write.rs:534`) |

The module doc (`probe.rs:9-15`) chose this deliberately over an index, but it is a growing fixed tax at the head of every push, and it is not cached (`cache-control: no-store`, `probe.rs:116`).

Auth cost per write request: `authorize_write` (`crates/cachet-worker/src/lib.rs:288-298` → `crates/cachet-worker/src/auth.rs:204-241`) does a full RS256 verify per request, plus a JWKS `fetch` on a cold isolate (`auth.rs:74-130`, TTL 10 min, `constants.rs:216`). Cheap relative to the above, but it is per-request and unmemoized on the write path (only the *read* path has the isolate memo, `verdict.rs:23-81`).

---

## 6. REQUEST COUNT — pushing ONE store path end to end

Per-run fixed cost (paid once regardless of path count, thanks to `RunTokens`, `crates/cachet-push/src/oidc.rs:121-149`):

1. `GET $ACTIONS_ID_TOKEN_REQUEST_URL&audience=…` — OIDC mint, `oidc.rs:86-98`. One per run (memoized; re-minted only on a 401).
2. `POST {cache}/api/probe` — `pipeline.rs:312-333`. One per run. Server-side cost = full bucket enumeration (§5).
3. `POST {cache}/roots/{project}` — `pipeline.rs:258-281`. One per run, default branch only.

Per path, small NAR (≤ ~90 MiB) — **2 HTTP requests**:

4. `PUT {cache}/nar/<52>.nar.zst` — `pipeline.rs:440-448`.
5. `PUT {cache}/<hash>.narinfo` — same code path, second phase. *(This is the one that costs the worker a full re-download + decode + double hash.)*

Per path, large NAR — **N + 3 HTTP requests**:

4. `POST {cache}/nar/<52>.nar.zst?uploads` with `x-cachet-upload-bytes` — `pipeline.rs:528-556`.
5. N × `PUT …?uploadId=<id>&partNumber=<n>` — `pipeline.rs:612-634`, 4-wide.
6. `POST …?uploadId=<id>` with the parts JSON — `pipeline.rs:560-588`.
7. `PUT {cache}/<hash>.narinfo`.
   (+ best-effort `DELETE …?uploadId=<id>` on failure, `pipeline.rs:639-654`.)

**Total for one small path, cold: 5 HTTP requests** (mint, probe, NAR PUT, narinfo PUT, lease). There is no presence HEAD per path anymore — commit `a9f5b46` replaced those with the bulk probe. So the request *count* is already lean; **the slowness is bytes, barriers, and the worker's inline re-verification, not chattiness** — with the one exception of the per-part record GET and the bucket-wide probe enumeration.

No local `nix copy`-side HTTP: staging is `file://`, so nix never talks to the cache.

---

## 7. Sleeps, backoff, polling

Retry envelope — `crates/cachet-push/src/retry.rs`:

```rust
// crates/cachet-push/src/retry.rs:6-21
pub const RETRY_MAX: u32 = 3;
pub const RETRY_BASE_DELAY_MS: u64 = 500;

pub fn attempt_delay_ms(tries: u32) -> u64 {
    RETRY_BASE_DELAY_MS * u64::from(tries + 1)
}

pub fn delay_after(tries: u32) -> Option<u64> {
    (tries + 1 < RETRY_MAX).then(|| attempt_delay_ms(tries))
}
```

Linear, not exponential: **500 ms then 1000 ms**, then fail. Driven by `with_retries`, `pipeline.rs:658-683`; the real sleeper is `tokio::time::sleep` (`crates/cachet-cli/src/push.rs:217-219`).

- **Every** wire operation is wrapped: probe (`pipeline.rs:313`), each single PUT (`pipeline.rs:442`), multipart begin (`pipeline.rs:530`), each part (`pipeline.rs:618`), complete (`pipeline.rs:567`), lease (`pipeline.rs:260`). Worst case per object = 3 attempts × full body + 1.5 s of sleep.
- **Retry amplification is severe on the narinfo PUT**: 3 attempts × (full R2 re-download + full zstd decode + double SHA-256) on the worker.
- A failing wave kills the run *and* discards all later waves (`pipeline.rs:359-362`), so a single flaky PUT in wave 1 of 20 wastes everything after it. The test at `crates/cachet-push/src/pipeflow.rs:887-945` codifies exactly this ("a failed NAR wave blocks the next wave").
- `abort_multipart` intentionally lets the whole failing wave finish before the DELETE (`pipeline.rs:509-515`) — a deliberate latency-for-determinism trade on the failure path.
- No polling loops on the push path (the device-flow poll in `crates/cachet-cli/src/login.rs` is login-only). The serial cursor loop at `crates/cachet-worker/src/probe.rs:70-99` is the closest thing, and it is unbounded in the inventory size.

---

## Ranked summary of what is actually costing time

1. **`nix copy` compresses the entire closure of every survivor into a fresh tempdir, then ~all of it is discarded** — `pipeline.rs:198-199` + `pipeline.rs:229-231`. CPU proportional to closure size, not delta. Silent (stderr captured, `real.rs:141`), no `compression-level`/`parallel-compression`, no streaming (disk write + disk read-back).
2. **The worker re-downloads and re-verifies the whole NAR inline on the narinfo PUT** — `write.rs:415-447`, `write.rs:568-641`. Full R2 re-read + WASM zstd decode + 2× SHA-256 per path, 16 concurrently, at the very end of the run, with 3× retry amplification.
3. **`POST /api/probe` enumerates the whole bucket serially** — `probe.rs:70-99`. O(inventory) at the head of every push.
4. **Large NARs are uploaded strictly one at a time** — the `for` loop at `pipeline.rs:412-414` — with only 4 × 64 MiB parts in flight (`pipeline.rs:27`, `constants.rs:146`).
5. **Barrier waves instead of a sliding window** — `pipeline.rs:352-364`; every wave pays its slowest member, and the 360 MiB byte budget (`pipeline.rs:23`) shrinks waves to as few as 4 when objects are large.
6. **Full in-memory buffering plus a per-attempt clone** — `pipeline.rs:444`, `pipeline.rs:620`, `real.rs:267-273`, `real.rs:289-296`. Up to ~720 MiB resident and a redundant memcpy of every byte uploaded.
7. **HTTP/1.1 only** (no `h2` in `Cargo.lock`) — 16 TLS handshakes per wave, no multiplexing, no configured pool/timeouts (`real.rs:21-29`).
8. **Per-part R2 record GET** on the worker — `write.rs:243` — one extra round trip per 64 MiB part.
9. **Two full `nix path-info --all` runs per job** (`push.rs:164` main step, `pipeline.rs:141` post step) plus sequential per-installable resolution that can fall through to a full flake evaluation (`real.rs:168-194`).

## CPU Time Limits

Free plan Workers have 10ms CPU time per request, while Paid plan Workers have up to 5 minutes of CPU time per request (30 seconds by default). For Cron Triggers, paid plans get 30 seconds of CPU time for intervals less than 1 hour and 15 minutes for intervals 1 hour or greater.

Paid plan Workers default to 30 seconds and can be raised up to 5 minutes (300,000ms) through configuration in your Wrangler file.

## Subrequest Limits

Workers on paid plans are limited to 10,000 subrequests per invocation by default, but this limit can be increased up to 10 million by setting the new subrequests limit in your Wrangler configuration file. The search results don't contain specific information about streaming limits for Workers in 2026. The CPU time limits apply regardless of whether you're using streaming, since CPU time measures how long the CPU spends executing Worker code, and waiting on network requests does not count toward CPU time.

Cloudflare R2 supports SHA-1, SHA-256, SHA-384, and SHA-512 checksums in put options.

## Key Store Parameters

For NAR compression method, you can use xz, bzip2, gzip, zstd, or none, with additional options including br, compress, grzip, lrzip, lz4, lzip, lzma or lzop in newer versions.

The compression-level parameter sets the preset level to be used when compressing NARs, with the meaning and accepted values depending on the compression method selected, and -1 specifying that the default compression level should be used.

**BUT — every cacheable NAR body is `tee()`d on a miss.** `read.rs:192-198`:

```rust
if is_edge_cacheable(size) {
    if let Some(cache_key) = cache_key {
        let cached = response.cloned()?;

```rust
let edge = web_sys::Response::from(&*self);
let cloned = edge.clone()?;
self.body = match edge.body() {
    Some(stream) => ResponseBody::Stream(stream),
    None => ResponseBody::Empty,

```rust
pub fn object_cache_key(generation: u64, request_path: &str) -> String {
    let path = request_path.strip_prefix('/').unwrap_or(request_path);
    format!("{EDGE_CACHE_KEY_ORIGIN}/g{generation}/{path}")

I found search results related to your query about Nix binary cache narinfo query performance. Here are the key findings:

## Overview

Nix uses persistent HTTP connections and lots of parallelism to look up .narinfo files efficiently. However, there have been performance challenges identified in how substituter queries are handled.

## Performance Bottlenecks

There have been investigations into why substitution (querying) is fairly slow, with HTTP/2 expected to handle large derivation sets in under a second. The async API for HTTP/2 wasn't fully utilized, and throughput is limited by the thread pool size used to fetch path infos in parallel. Performance can be improved by over 50x by massively scaling up that thread pool.

## HTTP Connections Tuning

The `http-connections` setting controls the maximum number of parallel TCP connections when fetching from binary caches. This is a configuration option that can be tuned to improve performance.

## Binary Cache Query Process

Every Nix Binary Cache supports querying for NARInfo files for a particular store path by taking the cryptographic hash portion and using it to fetch the metadata.

The search results indicate that while HTTP/2 should theoretically provide fast narinfo queries, the actual implementation has been limited by thread pool sizes rather than protocol capabilities, and adjusting the `http-connections` configuration can help optimize performance.

**Already parallel:** auth ∥ generation — `lib.rs:257-263` (`futures_util::future::join`). Nicely done.

**Still sequential, and each is a fixable round trip:**

1. **`Cache.get(object_key)` → `bucket.get(key)`** (`read.rs:156` then `read.rs:167`). These could race: fire the R2 get speculatively and cancel/ignore on cache hit. On an edge miss you serially pay both. Given §2 (daily full-cache invalidation), this is the common path more often than the design assumes.
2. **The generation resolution is serialized *ahead of* the object cache lookup**, not with it (`lib.rs:250-264` completes, then `read.rs:145` runs). Only the memo (`read.rs:90-94`) saves you.
3. **`authorize_read` → then everything.** Auth cannot race the R2 fetch today, because `read_routes` returns early on `Err` at `lib.rs:265-267` before `serve_object` is ever called. Based on the search results, here's what I found about Cloudflare Workers WebAssembly SIMD support:

## SIMD Support Status

SIMD is supported on Workers. This is confirmed in the official Cloudflare Workers documentation.

## Performance Considerations

According to research on WebAssembly SIMD performance, performance improvement is around 3x compared to scalar Wasm when SIMD is utilized effectively.

## Development Caveats

However, there are some important limitations to be aware of. While Cloudflare's platform is detected as Wasm SIMD enabled, there are practical constraints. Cloudflare has several caveats including poor developer experience with Wasm in JS, and users cannot freely compile Wasm inline within Workers JavaScript code - instead, Wasm modules must be uploaded as separate compiled files.

For cryptographic operations like SHA256, if you're planning to use SIMD-accelerated implementations, you would need to compile your Wasm module separately and then import it into your Worker, rather than writing and compiling inline.

input.content:
# Unfucking cachet's throughput

## Context

Pushes take twenty minutes and the cache is nearly empty as a result. I
measured the live deployment and the recent CI runs before touching anything.

**Reads are not the problem.** Against `cachet.nox.so` from Vancouver:

| Measurement | cachet | cache.nixos.org |
| --- | --- | --- |
| narinfo, warm edge | 38-52 ms | n/a |
| narinfo, cold | 120-150 ms | 133 ms |
| narinfo, 200 requests at concurrency 25 | 1.47 s | 1.32 s |
| NAR throughput | 38-42 MB/s | 50 MB/s |

The edge cache works (repeat reads fall 69 ms to 39 ms), 404s cache too
(198 ms to 37 ms), and curl sends Basic preemptively from netrc, so the
missing `WWW-Authenticate` header costs no round trip. The read path is at
rough parity with cache.nixos.org.

**Reads feel slow because the cache is empty.** Of 300 random local store
paths, cachet holds 12 and cache.nixos.org holds 71. cachet has priority 30,
so nix asks it first for every path in every closure, eats a 404, and falls
through to cache.nixos.org anyway. Every substitution pays an extra round trip
for a 4% hit rate.

**The cache is empty because writes are catastrophic.** From CI run 32803263823:

| Job | Build | Push |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `openapi` | 47 s | **31 min** (974 paths, 1948 objects) |
| `wasm` | 1 m 49 s | **18 min** (830 paths) |
| `unit` | 1 m 12 s | 57 s |

That is 1.34 seconds per object on the `openapi` job. The push step is forty
times the job it is supposed to accelerate, and pushes that slow do not finish,
which is why nothing lands.

The previous TypeScript implementation at `~/Development/cachet` was fast for
structural reasons, not because of tuning: its worker streamed request bodies
straight into R2 and did no hashing, no decompression, and no signature work at
all (signing was client-side through `nix copy --secret-key`). The Rust rewrite
moved signing server-side, which is the right call for the threat model, but
the verification it added runs inline on the critical path and re-reads every
byte it just stored.

## What is actually wrong

Ranked by measured cost.

**1. The worker re-downloads and re-verifies the whole NAR on every narinfo
PUT.** `crates/cachet-worker/src/write.rs:415-447`: `head()`, then a full
`bucket.get()` of the object the client uploaded seconds earlier, then
`measure_nar` (`write.rs:568-641`) streams all of it through a SHA-256 over the
compressed bytes, a ruzstd decode, and a second SHA-256 over every decompressed
byte. For rustc that is 132 MB re-read, 409 MB decoded, and 541 MB hashed, in
wasm, with no SIMD, per path. ruzstd runs 1.4x to 3.5x slower than C zstd. The
client retries three times, so a worker that runs out of CPU pays it three
times.

**2. Large NARs upload strictly one at a time.**
`crates/cachet-push/src/pipeline.rs:412-414` is a plain sequential `for` loop
over every multipart object, and multipart is exactly the set of fat NARs that
dominate wall time. Inside each, `PART_CONCURRENCY = 4` (`pipeline.rs:27`).

**3. `nix copy` compresses the whole closure and then the client throws it
away.** `pipeline.rs:198-199` stages survivors into a fresh tempdir, so nothing
is ever "already present" at the destination and nix re-serializes and re-zstds
every closure member, including everything the cache already holds.
`pipeline.rs:229-231` then filters almost all of it out. The comment at
`pipeline.rs:202-211` already names this problem; the filter just runs after the
CPU is spent. The step also prints nothing (`real.rs:141` captures stderr), so
the longest phase of the run is silent.

**4. Everything is buffered in memory and cloned per retry.** `real.rs:267-273`
reads whole objects with `tokio::fs::read`; `pipeline.rs:444` and
`pipeline.rs:620` `body.clone()` up to 90 MiB on every attempt. Peak resident
runs to ~720 MiB in a singles wave.

**5. Barrier waves, not a sliding window.** `wave_run`
(`pipeline.rs:346-365`) uses `join_all` per wave, so every wave costs its
slowest member and 15 finished slots idle behind one straggler.

**6. HTTP/1.1 only.** `reqwest` is built with `default-features = false` and no
`http2`; `h2` is absent from `Cargo.lock`. Sixteen concurrent PUTs mean sixteen
TLS handshakes and no multiplexing.

**7. The bulk probe enumerates the entire bucket on every push.**
`crates/cachet-worker/src/probe.rs:70-99` is a serial cursor-chained R2 list of
every root-level key, 1000 per page, uncached. Cost is O(inventory), paid at the
head of every push.

**8. The daily GC bump wipes the global edge cache.** `gc.rs:959-975` bumps the
generation whenever a sweep deletes anything, and the generation prefixes every
edge-cache key (`crates/cachet-core/src/generation.rs:71-74`). The cron is
daily, so the 30-day `immutable` TTL can never be realized past 24 hours.

**9. The wasm is built without SIMD or LTO.** There is no `[profile.release]`
in `Cargo.toml` and no `.cargo/config.toml`, so `worker-build --release` ships
stock `opt-level=3, lto=false, codegen-units=16`. Workers supports wasm SIMD,
worth roughly 3x on SHA-256 and a large gain on ruzstd.

**10. No observability, no CPU limit, no placement.**
`infra/alchemy.run.ts:41-72` sets none of `observability`, `limits.cpu_ms`, or
`placement`. The worker emits a rich event vocabulary that goes nowhere in
production, and the CPU ceiling sits at the 30 s default.

**11. Duplicate `Sig:` lines.** The live rustc narinfo carries the same cachet
signature twice. `with_signature` (`crates/cachet-core/src/narinfo.rs:200-207`)
appends unconditionally, and `nix copy` preserves Sig lines already in the local
store, so every push, substitute, re-push cycle appends another copy. The
narinfo grows until it hits `NARINFO_BYTES_MAX` (64 KiB) and pushes start
failing.

## The work

### Phase 1: the worker stops re-reading what it just stored

Measure during the write, not after it. This keeps verify-then-sign intact
(CLAUDE.md §1) and tightens it: the bytes measured become literally the bytes
stored, with no re-read gap.

- `crates/cachet-worker/src/write.rs`, `put_nar` (around `write.rs:82-91`):
  tee the incoming body stream through the existing `Sha256Stream` and
  `ZstdStream` (`cachet-crypto`) as it flows to R2, and record the measured
  facts (decompressed size, decompressed hash, compressed hash, compressed size)
  in the R2 object's custom metadata on `put`. Pass the client-declared
  compressed hash as R2's own `sha256` checksum option so R2 rejects a corrupt
  body itself, at no worker CPU cost.
- `put_narinfo` (`write.rs:388-497`): read those facts from the `head()` it
  already performs at `write.rs:415`, and delete the `bucket.get()` at
  `write.rs:425-435` and the `measure_nar` call at `write.rs:444`. Feed the
  metadata into the existing `VerifiedNar::verify`
  (`crates/cachet-core/src/write.rs:91-122`) unchanged, so the signer's input
  type is still the verifier's output.
- Multipart keeps the streaming re-read, because parts arrive out of order.
  That path now carries the cost alone instead of every path paying it. Also
  drop the per-part `load_record` R2 GET (`write.rs:243`) by folding the record
  read into the part handler's existing work.
- A NAR whose metadata is missing (uploaded before this change) falls back to
  the re-read path, so the bucket needs no migration.

### Phase 2: the client streams instead of staging

Replace the tempdir entirely, per the chosen approach.

- `crates/cachet-push/src/pipeline.rs:196-231`: delete the `copy_to` staging
  block, `read_staging_layout`, and the survivor filter that follows it.

**Reads are not the problem.** Against `cachet.nox.so` from Vancouver:

| Measurement | cachet | cache.nixos.org |
| --- | --- | --- |
| narinfo, warm edge | 38-52 ms | n/a |
| narinfo, cold | 120-150 ms | 133 ms |
| narinfo, 200 requests at concurrency 25 | 1.47 s | 1.32 s |
| NAR throughput | 38-42 MB/s | 50 MB/s |

(198 ms to 37 ms), and curl sends Basic preemptively from netrc, so the
missing `WWW-Authenticate` header costs no round trip. The read path is at
rough parity with cache.nixos.org.

**Reads feel slow because the cache is empty.** Of 300 random local store
paths, cachet holds 12 and cache.nixos.org holds 71. cachet has priority 30,
so nix asks it first for every path in every closure, eats a 404, and falls
through to cache.nixos.org anyway. Every substitution pays an extra round trip
for a 4% hit rate.

| Job | Build | Push |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `openapi` | 47 s | **31 min** (974 paths, 1948 objects) |
| `wasm` | 1 m 49 s | **18 min** (830 paths) |
| `unit` | 1 m 12 s | 57 s |

times the job it is supposed to accelerate, and pushes that slow do not finish,
which is why nothing lands.

The previous TypeScript implementation at `~/Development/cachet` was fast for
structural reasons, not because of tuning: its worker streamed request bodies
straight into R2 and did no hashing, no decompression, and no signature work at
all (signing was client-side through `nix copy --secret-key`). The Rust rewrite
moved signing server-side, which is the right call for the threat model, but
the verification it added runs inline on the critical path and re-reads every
byte it just stored.

## What is actually wrong

Ranked by measured cost.

**1. The worker re-downloads and re-verifies the whole NAR on every narinfo
PUT.** `crates/cachet-worker/src/write.rs:415-447`: `head()`, then a full
`bucket.get()` of the object the client uploaded seconds earlier, then

compressed bytes, a ruzstd decode, and a second SHA-256 over every decompressed
byte. For rustc that is 132 MB re-read, 409 MB decoded, and 541 MB hashed, in
wasm, with no SIMD, per path. ruzstd runs 1.4x to 3.5x slower than C zstd. The
client retries three times, so a worker that runs out of CPU pays it three
times.

**2. Large NARs upload strictly one at a time.**
`crates/cachet-push/src/pipeline.rs:412-414` is a plain sequential `for` loop
over every multipart object, and multipart is exactly the set of fat NARs that
dominate wall time. Inside each, `PART_CONCURRENCY = 4` (`pipeline.rs:27`).

**3. `nix copy` compresses the whole closure and then the client throws it

**4. Everything is buffered in memory and cloned per retry.** `real.rs:267-273`
reads whole objects with `tokio::fs::read`; `pipeline.rs:444` and

**5. Barrier waves, not a sliding window.** `wave_run`

**6. HTTP/1.1 only.** `reqwest` is built with `default-features = false` and no
`http2`; `h2` is absent from `Cargo.lock`. Sixteen concurrent PUTs mean sixteen
TLS handshakes and no multiplexing.

**7. The bulk probe enumerates the entire bucket on every push.**
