slowest member and 15 finished slots idle behind one straggler.

**6. HTTP/1.1 only.** `reqwest` is built with `default-features = false` and no
`http2`; `h2` is absent from `Cargo.lock`. Sixteen concurrent PUTs mean sixteen
TLS handshakes and no multiplexing.

**7. The bulk probe enumerates the entire bucket on every push.**
`crates/cachet-worker/src/probe.rs:70-99` is a serial cursor-chained R2 list of
every root-level key, 1000 per page, uncached. Cost is O(inventory), paid at the
head of every push.

**8. The daily GC bump wipes the global edge cache.** `gc.rs:959-975` bumps the
generation whenever a sweep deletes anything, and the generation prefixes every
edge-cache key (`crates/cachet-core/src/generation.rs:71-74`). The cron is
daily, so the 30-day `immutable` TTL can never be realized past 24 hours.

**9. The wasm is built without SIMD or LTO.** There is no `[profile.release]`
in `Cargo.toml` and no `.cargo/config.toml`, so `worker-build --release` ships
stock `opt-level=3, lto=false, codegen-units=16`. Workers supports wasm SIMD,
worth roughly 3x on SHA-256 and a large gain on ruzstd.

**10. No observability, no CPU limit, no placement.**
`infra/alchemy.run.ts:41-72` sets none of `observability`, `limits.cpu_ms`, or
`placement`. The worker emits a rich event vocabulary that goes nowhere in
production, and the CPU ceiling sits at the 30 s default.

**11. Duplicate `Sig:` lines.** The live rustc narinfo carries the same cachet
signature twice. `with_signature` (`crates/cachet-core/src/narinfo.rs:200-207`)
appends unconditionally, and `nix copy` preserves Sig lines already in the local
store, so every push, substitute, re-push cycle appends another copy. The
narinfo grows until it hits `NARINFO_BYTES_MAX` (64 KiB) and pushes start
failing.

## The work

### Phase 1: the worker stops re-reading what it just stored

Measure during the write, not after it. This keeps verify-then-sign intact
(CLAUDE.md §1) and tightens it: the bytes measured become literally the bytes
stored, with no re-read gap.

- `crates/cachet-worker/src/write.rs`, `put_nar` (around `write.rs:82-91`):
  tee the incoming body stream through the existing `Sha256Stream` and
  `ZstdStream` (`cachet-crypto`) as it flows to R2, and record the measured
  facts (decompressed size, decompressed hash, compressed hash, compressed size)
  in the R2 object's custom metadata on `put`. Pass the client-declared
  compressed hash as R2's own `sha256` checksum option so R2 rejects a corrupt
  body itself, at no worker CPU cost.
- `put_narinfo` (`write.rs:388-497`): read those facts from the `head()` it
  already performs at `write.rs:415`, and delete the `bucket.get()` at
  `write.rs:425-435` and the `measure_nar` call at `write.rs:444`. Feed the
  metadata into the existing `VerifiedNar::verify`
  (`crates/cachet-core/src/write.rs:91-122`) unchanged, so the signer's input
  type is still the verifier's output.
- Multipart keeps the streaming re-read, because parts arrive out of order.
  That path now carries the cost alone instead of every path paying it. Also
  drop the per-part `load_record` R2 GET (`write.rs:243`) by folding the record
  read into the part handler's existing work.
- A NAR whose metadata is missing (uploaded before this change) falls back to
  the re-read path, so the bucket needs no migration.

### Phase 2: the client streams instead of staging

Replace the tempdir entirely, per the chosen approach.

- `crates/cachet-push/src/pipeline.rs:196-231`: delete the `copy_to` staging
  block, `read_staging_layout`, and the survivor filter that follows it.
- `crates/cachet-push/src/real.rs`: add a `dump_path` command that spawns
  `nix dump-path <path>` and returns its stdout as a stream, and extend
  `path_info` to request `--json` so it yields `narHash`, `narSize`,
  `references`, and `deriver` directly.
- New per-path pipeline: for each survivor, stream `nix dump-path` through a
  zstd encoder into the PUT body, hashing the compressed bytes as they flow to
  produce `FileHash`/`FileSize`; then build the narinfo from the JSON facts plus
  the measured file facts and PUT it. Keep NAR-before-narinfo ordering per path;
  the worker enforces NEVER-DANGLE regardless, so no global barrier is needed.
- Strip any pre-existing `Sig:` lines from the constructed narinfo. Combined
  with the `with_signature` dedupe in Phase 4, this closes the duplicate-Sig
  growth.
- `crates/cachet-push/src/adapters.rs:67-74`: change the `Http` trait's body
  from `Vec<u8>` to a streaming body so nothing is buffered or cloned. The
  `stream` reqwest feature is already enabled and currently unused on the
  request side.
- Replace `wave_run` (`pipeline.rs:346-365`) with a sliding window
  (`buffer_unordered` over a bounded stream), sized by both path count and bytes
  in flight. Multipart objects join the same window rather than the sequential
  loop at `pipeline.rs:412-414`; parts get their own inner window.
- Enable `http2` on the reqwest client (`real.rs:21-29`) and set
  `pool_max_idle_per_host` so the window reuses connections.
- Print progress during the upload so a long push is legible.

### Phase 3: infrastructure and build

- `infra/alchemy.run.ts:41-72`: add `observability: { enabled: true }`,
  `limits: { cpu_ms: 300_000 }`, and `placement: { mode: "smart" }`. Without
  the first, none of this is measurable in production.
- `Cargo.toml`: add `[profile.release]` with `lto = "fat"`,
  `codegen-units = 1`, `panic = "abort"`. Add `.cargo/config.toml` with
  `-C target-feature=+simd128` for `wasm32-unknown-unknown`. Re-run
  `just wasm-hygiene`, which gates the shipped bundle (CLAUDE.md §5).

### Phase 4: the smaller correctness and cost fixes

- `crates/cachet-core/src/narinfo.rs:200-207`: dedupe in `with_signature` so a
  re-push cannot append a second identical signature. Add a unit-lane case.
- `crates/cachet-worker/src/probe.rs:70-99`: cache the enumerated inventory in
  the Cache API under the existing generation key space, so repeat probes inside
  one generation cost nothing. The generation already bumps on every sweep,
  which is exactly when the inventory changes.
- `crates/cachet-core/src/generation.rs:71-74`: split the key space. Positive
  object entries drop the generation prefix and keep the 30-day `immutable` TTL,
  because objects are content-addressed and their bytes never change. Only 404
  entries carry the generation, and their TTL is short anyway. Document the
  tradeoff in the ADR: a swept object can keep serving from a warm colo until
  its TTL expires.
- `crates/cachet-worker/src/verdict.rs:326`: move `cache_verdict` off the
  critical path into `ctx.wait_until`. Join the per-org membership loop at
  `verdict.rs:185-203` instead of awaiting each in turn.
- `crates/cachet-worker/src/read.rs:194`: the `Response::cloned()` tee couples
  the client's download rate to the colo cache write. Measure it once
  observability is on, and if it costs throughput, write the cache copy from a
  second R2 read inside `wait_until` instead.
- `crates/cachet-worker/src/error.rs:15-21`: add `WWW-Authenticate: Basic` to
  401s. Not a measured cost today, but it is what the protocol expects and a
  client that does not send preemptively would otherwise double its requests.
- `crates/cachet-push/src/retry.rs:6-21`: exponential backoff instead of linear,
  and more than three attempts now that a retry no longer re-sends a buffered
  body.

### Phase 5: release

Bump `cachet-version` in `action/action.yml:56`, tag, and cut the release, so
CI stops running the old client. Releases are immutable, so the tag is final
once pushed.

## Verification

1. `just unit`, `just property`, `just golden`, `just kani`, `just workerd`,
   `just deny`, `just wasm-hygiene`, `just clippy` all green. The workerd lane
   already covers the verify-then-sign pipeline end to end and the multipart
   quartet; extend it with a case asserting the NAR PUT records its measured
   facts and the narinfo PUT signs without a second object read, and a case
   asserting a re-pushed narinfo carries exactly one `Sig:` line.
2. Add a timing assertion to the workerd lane's CLI push scenario so a
   regression in push wall time fails a lane rather than surfacing in CI weeks
   later. Register it in `docs/testing/lanes.toml` if it becomes its own lane
   (CLAUDE.md §0 and §8: the verb, the CI job, and the doc row land together).
3. Deploy to staging, run `just integration`, and compare the post-step push
   time against the 5 m 18 s baseline from run 32806212498 for the same closure.
4. On a green main, compare the `openapi` and `wasm` jobs' push steps against
   their 31-minute and 18-minute baselines from run 32803263823.
5. Re-run the coverage measurement: `curl` 300 random local store hashes against
   `/{hash}.narinfo` and confirm the hit rate climbs off 4% as pushes start
   completing.
6. With observability on, confirm from the worker's own event stream that
   `read.edge_hit` dominates `read.bucket_hit` after a GC sweep, which it cannot
   do today.

## Documentation

CLAUDE.md §8 gates three bijections, so these land in the same commits as the
code:

- An ADR for moving measurement into the write (the invariant is unchanged, the
  mechanism is not), and one for the edge-cache key split.
- `docs/testing/workerd.md` gains the new scenarios; `docs/testing/lanes.toml`
  stays in step with `check-lane-manifest.sh`.
- `docs/security/threat-model.md`: the poisoned-narinfo scenario's "Proven"
  line changes from a re-read to a measured-during-write proof.
- `docs/DEPLOY.md`: note the new worker limits and observability.
- Any new Markdown file joins the §11 manifest, per `check-doc-manifest.sh`.

# Unfucking cachet's throughput

## Context

Pushes take twenty minutes and the cache is nearly empty as a result. I
measured the live deployment and the recent CI runs before touching anything.

**Reads are not the problem.** Against `cachet.nox.so` from Vancouver:

| Measurement | cachet | cache.nixos.org |
| --- | --- | --- |
| narinfo, warm edge | 38-52 ms | n/a |
| narinfo, cold | 120-150 ms | 133 ms |
| narinfo, 200 requests at concurrency 25 | 1.47 s | 1.32 s |
| NAR throughput | 38-42 MB/s | 50 MB/s |

The edge cache works (repeat reads fall 69 ms to 39 ms), 404s cache too
(198 ms to 37 ms), and curl sends Basic preemptively from netrc, so the
missing `WWW-Authenticate` header costs no round trip. The read path is at
rough parity with cache.nixos.org.

**Reads feel slow because the cache is empty.** Of 300 random local store
paths, cachet holds 12 and cache.nixos.org holds 71. cachet has priority 30,
so nix asks it first for every path in every closure, eats a 404, and falls
through to cache.nixos.org anyway. Every substitution pays an extra round trip
for a 4% hit rate.

**The cache is empty because writes are catastrophic.** From CI run 32803263823:

| Job | Build | Push |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `openapi` | 47 s | **31 min** (974 paths, 1948 objects) |
| `wasm` | 1 m 49 s | **18 min** (830 paths) |
| `unit` | 1 m 12 s | 57 s |

That is 1.34 seconds per object on the `openapi` job. The push step is forty
times the job it is supposed to accelerate, and pushes that slow do not finish,
which is why nothing lands.

The previous TypeScript implementation at `~/Development/cachet` was fast for
structural reasons, not because of tuning: its worker streamed request bodies
straight into R2 and did no hashing, no decompression, and no signature work at
all (signing was client-side through `nix copy --secret-key`). The Rust rewrite
moved signing server-side, which is the right call for the threat model, but
the verification it added runs inline on the critical path and re-reads every
byte it just stored.

## What is actually wrong

Ranked by measured cost.

**1. The worker re-downloads and re-verifies the whole NAR on every narinfo
PUT.** `crates/cachet-worker/src/write.rs:415-447`: `head()`, then a full
`bucket.get()` of the object the client uploaded seconds earlier, then
`measure_nar` (`write.rs:568-641`) streams all of it through a SHA-256 over the
compressed bytes, a ruzstd decode, and a second SHA-256 over every decompressed
byte. For rustc that is 132 MB re-read, 409 MB decoded, and 541 MB hashed, in
wasm, with no SIMD, per path. ruzstd runs 1.4x to 3.5x slower than C zstd. The
client retries three times, so a worker that runs out of CPU pays it three
times.

**2. Large NARs upload strictly one at a time.**
`crates/cachet-push/src/pipeline.rs:412-414` is a plain sequential `for` loop
over every multipart object, and multipart is exactly the set of fat NARs that
dominate wall time. Inside each, `PART_CONCURRENCY = 4` (`pipeline.rs:27`).

**3. `nix copy` compresses the whole closure and then the client throws it
away.** `pipeline.rs:198-199` stages survivors into a fresh tempdir, so nothing
is ever "already present" at the destination and nix re-serializes and re-zstds
every closure member, including everything the cache already holds.
`pipeline.rs:229-231` then filters almost all of it out. The comment at
`pipeline.rs:202-211` already names this problem; the filter just runs after the
CPU is spent. The step also prints nothing (`real.rs:141` captures stderr), so
the longest phase of the run is silent.

**4. Everything is buffered in memory and cloned per retry.** `real.rs:267-273`
reads whole objects with `tokio::fs::read`; `pipeline.rs:444` and
`pipeline.rs:620` `body.clone()` up to 90 MiB on every attempt. Peak resident
runs to ~720 MiB in a singles wave.

**5. Barrier waves, not a sliding window.** `wave_run`
(`pipeline.rs:346-365`) uses `join_all` per wave, so every wave costs its
slowest member and 15 finished slots idle behind one straggler.

**6. HTTP/1.1 only.** `reqwest` is built with `default-features = false` and no
`http2`; `h2` is absent from `Cargo.lock`. Sixteen concurrent PUTs mean sixteen
TLS handshakes and no multiplexing.

**7. The bulk probe enumerates the entire bucket on every push.**
`crates/cachet-worker/src/probe.rs:70-99` is a serial cursor-chained R2 list of
every root-level key, 1000 per page, uncached. Cost is O(inventory), paid at the
head of every push.

**8. The daily GC bump wipes the global edge cache.** `gc.rs:959-975` bumps the
generation whenever a sweep deletes anything, and the generation prefixes every
edge-cache key (`crates/cachet-core/src/generation.rs:71-74`). The cron is
daily, so the 30-day `immutable` TTL can never be realized past 24 hours.

**9. The wasm is built without SIMD or LTO.** There is no `[profile.release]`
in `Cargo.toml` and no `.cargo/config.toml`, so `worker-build --release` ships
stock `opt-level=3, lto=false, codegen-units=16`. Workers supports wasm SIMD,
worth roughly 3x on SHA-256 and a large gain on ruzstd.

**10. No observability, no CPU limit, no placement.**
`infra/alchemy.run.ts:41-72` sets none of `observability`, `limits.cpu_ms`, or
`placement`. The worker emits a rich event vocabulary that goes nowhere in
production, and the CPU ceiling sits at the 30 s default.

**11. Duplicate `Sig:` lines.** The live rustc narinfo carries the same cachet
signature twice. `with_signature` (`crates/cachet-core/src/narinfo.rs:200-207`)
appends unconditionally, and `nix copy` preserves Sig lines already in the local
store, so every push, substitute, re-push cycle appends another copy. The
narinfo grows until it hits `NARINFO_BYTES_MAX` (64 KiB) and pushes start
failing.

## The work

### Phase 1: the worker stops re-reading what it just stored

Measure during the write, not after it. This keeps verify-then-sign intact
(CLAUDE.md §1) and tightens it: the bytes measured become literally the bytes
stored, with no re-read gap.

through to cache.nixos.org anyway. Every substitution pays an extra round trip

CPU is spent. The step also prints nothing (`real.rs:141` captures stderr), so
the longest phase of the run is silent.

**4. Everything is buffered in memory and cloned per retry.** `real.rs:267-273`
reads whole objects with `tokio::fs::read`; `pipeline.rs:444` and
`pipeline.rs:620` `body.clone()` up to 90 MiB on every attempt. Peak resident
runs to ~720 MiB in a singles wave.

**5. Barrier waves, not a sliding window.** `wave_run`
(`pipeline.rs:346-365`) uses `join_all` per wave, so every wave costs its
slowest member and 15 finished slots idle behind one straggler.

**6. HTTP/1.1 only.** `reqwest` is built with `default-features = false` and no
`http2`; `h2` is absent from `Cargo.lock`. Sixteen concurrent PUTs mean sixteen
TLS handshakes and no multiplexing.

**7. The bulk probe enumerates the entire bucket on every push.**
`crates/cachet-worker/src/probe.rs:70-99` is a serial cursor-chained R2 list of
every root-level key, 1000 per page, uncached. Cost is O(inventory), paid at the
head of every push.

**8. The daily GC bump wipes the global edge cache.** `gc.rs:959-975` bumps the
generation whenever a sweep deletes anything, and the generation prefixes every
edge-cache key (`crates/cachet-core/src/generation.rs:71-74`). The cron is
daily, so the 30-day `immutable` TTL can never be realized past 24 hours.

**9. The wasm is built without SIMD or LTO.** There is no `[profile.release]`
in `Cargo.toml` and no `.cargo/config.toml`, so `worker-build --release` ships
stock `opt-level=3, lto=false, codegen-units=16`. Workers supports wasm SIMD,
worth roughly 3x on SHA-256 and a large gain on ruzstd.

**10. No observability, no CPU limit, no placement.**
`infra/alchemy.run.ts:41-72` sets none of `observability`, `limits.cpu_ms`, or
`placement`. The worker emits a rich event vocabulary that goes nowhere in
production, and the CPU ceiling sits at the 30 s default.

**11. Duplicate `Sig:` lines.** The live rustc narinfo carries the same cachet
signature twice. `with_signature` (`crates/cachet-core/src/narinfo.rs:200-207`)
appends unconditionally, and `nix copy` preserves Sig lines already in the local
store, so every push, substitute, re-push cycle appends another copy. The
narinfo grows until it hits `NARINFO_BYTES_MAX` (64 KiB) and pushes start
failing.

## The work

### Phase 1: the worker stops re-reading what it just stored

Measure during the write, not after it. This keeps verify-then-sign intact
(CLAUDE.md §1) and tightens it: the bytes measured become literally the bytes
stored, with no re-read gap.

- `crates/cachet-worker/src/write.rs`, `put_nar` (around `write.rs:82-91`):
  tee the incoming body stream through the existing `Sha256Stream` and
  `ZstdStream` (`cachet-crypto`) as it flows to R2, and record the measured
  facts (decompressed size, decompressed hash, compressed hash, compressed size)
  in the R2 object's custom metadata on `put`. Pass the client-declared
  compressed hash as R2's own `sha256` checksum option so R2 rejects a corrupt
  body itself, at no worker CPU cost.
- `put_narinfo` (`write.rs:388-497`): read those facts from the `head()` it
  already performs at `write.rs:415`, and delete the `bucket.get()` at
  `write.rs:425-435` and the `measure_nar` call at `write.rs:444`. Feed the
  metadata into the existing `VerifiedNar::verify`
  (`crates/cachet-core/src/write.rs:91-122`) unchanged, so the signer's input
  type is still the verifier's output.
- Multipart keeps the streaming re-read, because parts arrive out of order.
  That path now carries the cost alone instead of every path paying it. Also
  drop the per-part `load_record` R2 GET (`write.rs:243`) by folding the record
  read into the part handler's existing work.
- No fallback for objects lacking the metadata. The deployment is destroyed and
  recreated before this ships, so the bucket starts empty and every object in it
  was written by the new path. A NAR without measured facts is a typed error,
  not a slow path.

### Phase 2: the client streams instead of staging

Replace the tempdir entirely, per the chosen approach.

- `crates/cachet-push/src/pipeline.rs:196-231`: delete the `copy_to` staging
  block, `read_staging_layout`, and the survivor filter that follows it.
- `crates/cachet-push/src/real.rs`: add a `dump_path` command that spawns
  `nix dump-path <path>` and returns its stdout as a stream, and extend
  `path_info` to request `--json` so it yields `narHash`, `narSize`,
  `references`, and `deriver` directly.
- New per-path pipeline: for each survivor, stream `nix dump-path` through a
  zstd encoder into the PUT body, hashing the compressed bytes as they flow to
  produce `FileHash`/`FileSize`; then build the narinfo from the JSON facts plus
  the measured file facts and PUT it. Keep NAR-before-narinfo ordering per path;
  the worker enforces NEVER-DANGLE regardless, so no global barrier is needed.
- Strip any pre-existing `Sig:` lines from the constructed narinfo. Combined
  with the `with_signature` dedupe in Phase 4, this closes the duplicate-Sig
  growth.
- `crates/cachet-push/src/adapters.rs:67-74`: change the `Http` trait's body
  from `Vec<u8>` to a streaming body so nothing is buffered or cloned. The
  `stream` reqwest feature is already enabled and currently unused on the
  request side.
- Replace `wave_run` (`pipeline.rs:346-365`) with a sliding window
  (`buffer_unordered` over a bounded stream), sized by both path count and bytes
  in flight. Multipart objects join the same window rather than the sequential
  loop at `pipeline.rs:412-414`; parts get their own inner window.
- Enable `http2` on the reqwest client (`real.rs:21-29`) and set
  `pool_max_idle_per_host` so the window reuses connections.
- Print progress during the upload so a long push is legible.

### Phase 3: infrastructure and build

- `infra/alchemy.run.ts:41-72`: add `observability: { enabled: true }`,
  `limits: { cpu_ms: 300_000 }`, and `placement: { mode: "smart" }`. Without
  the first, none of this is measurable in production.
- `Cargo.toml`: add `[profile.release]` with `lto = "fat"`,
  `codegen-units = 1`, `panic = "abort"`. Add `.cargo/config.toml` with
  `-C target-feature=+simd128` for `wasm32-unknown-unknown`. Re-run
  `just wasm-hygiene`, which gates the shipped bundle (CLAUDE.md §5).

### Phase 4: the smaller correctness and cost fixes

- `crates/cachet-core/src/narinfo.rs:200-207`: dedupe in `with_signature` so a
  re-push cannot append a second identical signature. Add a unit-lane case. The
  stored narinfos that already carry duplicates go away with the bucket.
- `crates/cachet-worker/src/probe.rs:70-99`: cache the enumerated inventory in
  the Cache API under the existing generation key space, so repeat probes inside
  one generation cost nothing. The generation already bumps on every sweep,
  which is exactly when the inventory changes.
- `crates/cachet-core/src/generation.rs:71-74`: split the key space. Positive
  object entries drop the generation prefix and keep the 30-day `immutable` TTL,
  because objects are content-addressed and their bytes never change. Only 404
  entries carry the generation, and their TTL is short anyway. Document the
  tradeoff in the ADR: a swept object can keep serving from a warm colo until
  its TTL expires.
- `crates/cachet-worker/src/verdict.rs:326`: move `cache_verdict` off the
  critical path into `ctx.wait_until`. Join the per-org membership loop at
  `verdict.rs:185-203` instead of awaiting each in turn.
- `crates/cachet-worker/src/read.rs:194`: the `Response::cloned()` tee couples
  the client's download rate to the colo cache write. Measure it once
  observability is on, and if it costs throughput, write the cache copy from a
  second R2 read inside `wait_until` instead.
- `crates/cachet-worker/src/error.rs:15-21`: add `WWW-Authenticate: Basic` to
  401s. Not a measured cost today, but it is what the protocol expects and a
  client that does not send preemptively would otherwise double its requests.
- `crates/cachet-push/src/retry.rs:6-21`: exponential backoff instead of linear,
  and more than three attempts now that a retry no longer re-sends a buffered
  body.

### Phase 5: ship it

Everything above lands as one pull request against `main`, including the
version bump: `cachet-version` in `action/action.yml:56` and the workspace
version. After the merge, tag and cut the release so CI stops running the old
client. Releases are immutable, so the tag is final once pushed.

The existing deployment is destroyed and recreated rather than converged, so the
bucket, the KV namespace, and the generation counter all start clean. That means
no migration code anywhere: no metadata fallback in the worker, no duplicate-Sig
cleanup pass over stored narinfos, and no compatibility with the old edge-cache
key space. `just destroy production` then `just deploy production`, with the
signing key carried over from `infra/.env.production` so the deployment's
identity and the public key clients already trust do not move.

# cargo-deny: the supply-chain gate, run by `just deny`. Every dependency is
# attack surface, so the set is held to four checks: no known advisory, only
# accepted licenses, no banned or duplicated crates, and crates.io as the
# only source.

[advisories]
version = 2
# A new advisory can land against an unchanged tree, so this check is a
# time-varying signal: a `just deny` failure here means triage now, not
# necessarily a regression in the change under review.
yanked = "deny"
# Each ignore is a deliberate, justified triage decision, revisited whenever
# the dependency tree changes. An entry names the advisory and proves the
# vulnerable path is unreachable here.
ignore = [
    # `paste` is unmaintained, not vulnerable: a compile-time proc-macro
    # helper pulled in by hegeltest, the property lane's engine. It is a
    # dev-graph dependency: its generated code appears only in test binaries
    # and never enters the shipped worker. No replacement exists on the
    # pinned hegeltest version; the entry dies with the crate when the tree
    # moves.
    "RUSTSEC-2024-0436",
    # The Marvin advisory covers RSA private-key operations (decrypt and
    # sign) leaking through timing. cachet has no private RSA key anywhere:
    # the only RSA use is PUBLIC-key verification of GitHub OIDC tokens
    # against presented JWKs, in tests and in the worker alike, so the
    # vulnerable path is unreachable on every target.
    "RUSTSEC-2023-0071",
]

[licenses]
version = 2
# Permissive licenses only. cachet ships as Apache-2.0 open source; copyleft
# and unknown terms are refused so downstream redistribution stays simple.
allow = [
    "MIT",
    "Apache-2.0",
    "Apache-2.0 WITH LLVM-exception",
    "BSD-2-Clause",
    "BSD-3-Clause",
    "ISC",
    "Unicode-3.0",
    "Zlib",
    # why: the BSD Zero Clause license is OSI-approved and strictly more
    # permissive than MIT (public-domain-equivalent, no attribution
    # required), so it carries no obligation at all.
    "0BSD",
    # why: CDLA-Permissive is the Linux Foundation's permissive data
    # license, attribution-only with no copyleft. Its consumer is
    # webpki-roots, the TLS certificate bundle of the native crates.
    "CDLA-Permissive-2.0",
]
confidence-threshold = 0.93
# why: the workspace crates are publish = false; they are the product being
# built, not dependencies, so the license check skips them.
private = { ignore = true }

[bans]
# A duplicate major version is two copies of attack surface and a larger
# bundle; flag it so a single version is chosen deliberately. A wildcard
# version is refused outright: a dependency pins to a real range.
multiple-versions = "warn"
wildcards = "deny"
# The internal crates depend on each other by path, which has no version and
# reads as a wildcard; the ban still applies to external crates.
allow-wildcard-paths = true
# aws-lc and the C zstd crate do not build for wasm32-unknown-unknown;
# ruzstd supplies the worker's only decompression need. ring carries the
# same incompatibility, but the two native crates (cachet-push, cachet-cli)

# or aws-lc, so ring is allowed through exactly the rustls chain and no
# further: a new dependant outside these wrappers fails the gate, and the
# worker's artifact is scanned for it regardless (§5, check-wasm-hygiene).
deny = [
    { name = "ring", reason = "does not build for wasm32-unknown-unknown; allowed only as the rustls chain's native TLS provider", wrappers = ["rustls", "rustls-webpki"] },
    { name = "aws-lc-rs", reason = "does not build for wasm32-unknown-unknown" },
    { name = "aws-lc-sys", reason = "does not build for wasm32-unknown-unknown" },

    { name = "zstd-sys", reason = "C library, does not build for wasm32-unknown-unknown; use ruzstd" },
]

deny ok

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# The shipped-artifact hygiene gate (CLAUDE.md §5). The worker bundle must
# never carry ring, aws-lc, the C zstd library, or tokio symbols: deny.toml
# bans them from the
# graph, and this script catches anything that reaches the artifact anyway.
# It also scans the bundle for secret-shaped strings, because a leaked
# constant here ships to an edge runtime. Run after `just wasm`; the build
# output is the input, so the script fails with instructions when it is
# missing.
set -euo pipefail
export LC_ALL=C
cd "$(dirname "$0")/.."

BUILD="crates/cachet-worker/build"
if [ ! -d "$BUILD" ]; then
  echo "[wasm-hygiene] $BUILD not found; run 'just wasm' first" >&2
  exit 2
fi

wasm="$(find "$BUILD" -name '*.wasm' -print -quit)"
if [ -z "$wasm" ]; then
  echo "[wasm-hygiene] no .wasm module under $BUILD" >&2
  exit 2
fi

# why: bare "ring" matches std's string::String, so the patterns require a
# crate-qualified shape: the banned names appear as `::ring::`, `aws_lc_`,
# `zstd_sys`, the C library's own `ZSTD_` exports,
# or `::tokio::` when those runtimes leak into the module.
banned="$(wasm-tools print "$wasm" | grep -E ':(ring|tokio)::|aws_lc|aws-lc|zstd_sys|ZSTD_' || true)"
if [ -n "$banned" ]; then
  echo "[wasm-hygiene] banned runtime symbols in $wasm:" >&2
  printf '%s\n' "$banned" | head -20 >&2
  exit 1
fi

63	wildcards = "deny"

65	# reads as a wildcard; the ban still applies to external crates.
66	allow-wildcard-paths = true
67	# aws-lc, ring, and the C zstd crate do not build for
68	# wasm32-unknown-unknown, so none of them may reach the worker. Each is
69	# still needed by the two native crates (cachet-push, cachet-cli), which
70	# compile only for hosts, so each is allowed through exactly one named

72	# gate. ring is rustls's provider, because rustls's only remaining

      // belongs near them rather than near the client. Streaming a NAR
      // body is unaffected either way, and the cold read path's several

      placement: { mode: "smart" },'''

# aborting on panic drops the unwinding tables from a bundle that has no

1	//! Named wire constants shared by every crate (CLAUDE.md §4, §6). Bounds
2	//! stay here so the worker, the CLI, and the action cannot disagree about a
3	//! limit by drifting copies. Every constant cites the reason for its value.
4	
5	/// The exact body of `GET /nix-cache-info`. Priority 30 sorts cachet ahead
6	/// of cache.nixos.org (priority 40) in a client's substituter order, and
7	/// WantMassQuery permits nix to batch narinfo lookups.
8	pub const NIX_CACHE_INFO: &str = "StoreDir: /nix/store\nWantMassQuery: 1\nPriority: 30\n";
9	
10	/// The nix base32 alphabet: lowercase, excluding e, o, u, and t. Store-path
11	/// hashes are 32 chars; NAR file hashes are 52.
12	pub const NIX_BASE32_ALPHABET: &str = "REDACTED";
13	
14	/// Store-path hashes carry exactly this many nix base32 characters.
15	pub const STORE_PATH_HASH_LENGTH: usize = 32;
16	
17	/// NAR file hashes carry exactly this many nix base32 characters.
18	pub const NAR_FILE_HASH_LENGTH: usize = 52;
19	
20	/// The store directory every cachet narinfo names.
21	pub const NIX_STORE_DIR: &str = "/nix/store";
22	
23	/// A store path's name half: letters, digits, and `+-._?=`. Nix admits
24	/// exactly this set, and it excludes `/`, which is what stops a name from
25	/// smuggling a path segment.
26	pub const STORE_PATH_NAME_PATTERN: &str = r"^[a-zA-Z0-9+._?=-]+$";
27	
28	/// The longest store path name cachet accepts. 211 matches nixpkgs'
29	/// longest known name plus headroom; nix itself never publishes longer.
30	pub const STORE_PATH_NAME_BYTES_MAX: usize = 211;
31	
32	/// The suffix identifying a narinfo object.
33	pub const NARINFO_KEY_SUFFIX: &str = ".narinfo";
34	
35	/// The prefix under which every NAR object lives.
36	pub const NAR_KEY_PREFIX: &str = "nar/";
37	
38	/// The compression suffixes nix appends to a NAR key, by `Compression`
39	/// field value. Read paths accept exactly this set; the signing path
40	/// accepts only `""` and `.zst`.
41	pub const NAR_SUFFIXES: [&str; 8] = ["", ".xz", ".zst", ".bz2", ".gz", ".br", ".lzip", ".lz4"];
42	
43	/// The longest legal key is well under 70 bytes; anything over 128 is
44	/// refused by a length comparison before any pattern scan runs.
45	pub const KEY_BYTES_MAX: usize = 128;
46	
47	/// A narinfo body larger than this is refused with body_too_large: narinfos
48	/// are a few hundred bytes in practice, so 64 KiB is generous headroom and
49	/// still a hard guard in front of the parser.
50	pub const NARINFO_BYTES_MAX: u64 = 65_536;
51	
52	/// A narinfo with more lines than this is refused: the parser's work stays
53	/// linear and bounded regardless of content.
54	pub const NARINFO_LINES_MAX: usize = 2_048;
55	
56	/// One narinfo may name at most this many references. Caps both the parse
57	/// and the closure walk's fan-out per node.
58	pub const NARINFO_REFERENCES_MAX: usize = 1_024;
59	
60	/// The roots (lease renewal) payload is at most this many bytes: it is a
61	/// lease, not a bulk upload channel.
62	pub const ROOTS_BODY_BYTES_MAX: u64 = 524_288;
63	
64	/// A roots payload carries at most this many store paths or installables,
65	/// matching the push pipeline's closure cap.
66	pub const ROOTS_PATHS_MAX: usize = 4_096;
67	
68	/// A probe payload is at most this many bytes: `PUSH_PATHS_MAX` hashes
69	/// serialize to ~600 KB, so 1 MiB is headroom, and the byte cap answers
70	/// before the parser runs. The entry cap itself is `PUSH_PATHS_MAX`
71	/// shared with the push pipeline: one number, one truth, both sides.
72	pub const PROBE_BODY_BYTES_MAX: u64 = 1_048_576;
73	
74	/// The collector enumerates at most this many project leases per run.
75	pub const ROOTS_PROJECTS_MAX: usize = 256;
76	
77	/// An Authorization header longer than this is refused as malformed_auth:
78	/// JWTs run a few kilobytes, so 8 KiB is generous room while still a hard
79	/// guard in front of the parsers.
80	pub const AUTH_HEADER_BYTES_MAX: usize = 8_192;
81	
82	/// The nix `Compression` value narinfos default to when the field is
83	/// absent.
84	pub const DEFAULT_COMPRESSION: &str = "bzip2";
85	
86	/// The sentinel value for provenance fields missing from a lease: claims
87	/// old documents may predate, readable as absence rather than as truth.
88	pub const UNKNOWN_CLAIM: &str = "unknown";
89	
90	/// A project name is at most this long. GitHub caps an owner at 39
91	/// characters and a repository at 100, so 140 covers the longest
92	/// owner-repository default that can exist.
93	pub const PROJECT_NAME_BYTES_MAX: usize = 140;
94	
95	/// A project name: alphanumerics, dots, underscores, and dashes, starting
96	/// alphanumeric; never containing `..`.
97	pub const PROJECT_NAME_PATTERN: &str = r"^[A-Za-z0-9][A-Za-z0-9._-]*$";
98	
99	/// One lease document per project under this prefix.
100	pub const ROOTS_KEY_PREFIX: &str = "roots/";
101	
102	/// In-flight multipart bookkeeping lives under this prefix, unreachable
103	/// from any request by construction.
104	pub const UPLOADS_KEY_PREFIX: &str = "uploads/";
105	
106	/// The GC's per-run stage artifacts live under this prefix.
107	pub const GC_RUNS_KEY_PREFIX: &str = "gc-runs/";
108	
109	/// The GC's run reports live under this prefix.
110	pub const GC_REPORTS_KEY_PREFIX: &str = "gc-reports/";
111	
112	/// The edge-cache generation document's key.
113	pub const GENERATION_OBJECT_KEY: &str = "meta/generation";
114	
115	/// A stored NAR's measured facts live under the reserved meta prefix,
116	/// keyed by the NAR's own bucket key: `meta/nar/<hash>.nar.zst` records
117	/// what `nar/<hash>.nar.zst` measured when it landed.
118	pub const NAR_FACTS_KEY_PREFIX: &str = "meta/";
119	
120	/// A facts document is two hashes and two integers; anything approaching
121	/// this is not one, and the cap precedes the read.
122	pub const NAR_FACTS_BYTES_MAX: u64 = 512;
123	
124	/// A NAR write declares how many bytes its frame decodes to, and the
125	/// decoder is bounded by that declaration. This is the ceiling on the
126	/// declaration itself: no single store path decompresses past it, and the
127	/// bound has to exist before the decode starts or it is not a bound.
128	pub const NAR_DECOMPRESSED_BYTES_MAX: u64 = 68_719_476_736;
129	
130	/// The decoder is bounded a second time, by how far the stored bytes may
131	/// expand. A declaration is attacker-chosen, so on its own it lets a tiny
132	/// upload ask for an enormous decode; pairing it with a ratio means a
133	/// compression bomb can only spend CPU in proportion to the bytes it
134	/// actually uploaded. Real NARs of ordinary store paths land near 3x and
135	/// even a tree of mostly zeroes stays well under this.
136	pub const NAR_EXPANSION_RATIO_MAX: u64 = 200;
137	
138	/// A well-formed generation document is under a hundred bytes; anything
139	/// approaching 256 is corrupt, and the read path bypasses the edge cache
140	/// rather than trusting it.
141	pub const GENERATION_DOCUMENT_BYTES_MAX: u64 = 256;
142	
143	/// The internal prefixes that requests can never address. Key validation
144	/// makes these unreachable from a request; the sweep's candidate filter
145	/// refuses them a second time, because deletion is unrecoverable.
146	pub const RESERVED_KEY_PREFIXES: [&str; 5] = [
147	    ROOTS_KEY_PREFIX,
148	    UPLOADS_KEY_PREFIX,
149	    GC_RUNS_KEY_PREFIX,
150	    GC_REPORTS_KEY_PREFIX,
151	    "meta/",
152	];
153	
154	/// Single-shot NAR PUT refuses bodies larger than this with body_too_large:
155	/// 90 MiB of headroom under Cloudflare's 100 MB edge request cap. Larger
156	/// NARs use the multipart routes.
157	pub const UPLOAD_SINGLE_MAX_BYTES: u64 = 94_371_800;
158	
159	/// A multipart completion body: 1000 parts at 256 bytes each is room to
160	/// spare, and the cap exists so the parser's bound precedes the read.
161	pub const COMPLETE_BODY_BYTES_MAX: u64 = 262_144;
162	
163	/// An upload bookkeeping record: four small fields; anything larger is
164	/// not one.
165	pub const UPLOAD_RECORD_BYTES_MAX: u64 = 1_024;
166	
167	/// Every multipart part except the last is exactly this size; the last is
168	/// the declared remainder.
169	pub const UPLOAD_PART_BYTES: u64 = 67_108_864;

content.content:
# ADR 0011: Deployments are named, and the name is housekeeping

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-08-21
- **Context doc:** [../DEPLOY.md](../DEPLOY.md); supersedes the stage
  grammar of [ADR 0009](0009-alchemy-deployments.md) (its isolation and
  idempotence decisions stand)

## Context

cachet is self-hosted: every operator runs their own deployments, and an
operator may run several in one account (a staging rehearsal, multiple
production caches for different orgs). ADR 0009 framed stages as the
fixed pair `staging`/`production` and special-cased production:
only it defaulted its domain to the host, every other stage refused
without `CACHET_DEPLOY_DOMAIN`, and GC grace defaulted by stage name.
When deployments became a user-facing concept, the fixed pair could not
express "four production deployments in this account", and the
name-keyed special cases pushed deploy behavior into string comparisons.

## Decision

1. A deployment has an operator-chosen name matching
   `^[a-z][a-z0-9-]{1,31}$`, asked for first at `just bootstrap`. The
   name drives the env file (`infra/.env.<name>`), the alchemy stage,
   and the resource names (`cachet-<name>`; the prefix is a guarantee,
   not a ritual — a name already starting with `cachet-` is used as-is,
   so no stack ever reads `cachet-cachet-*`). `infra/src/config.ts`
   enforces the grammar on every deploy, so hand-written env files obey
   it too.
=== README index
# Architecture decision records

Each ADR records one decision: the context that forced it, the decision
itself, the consequences accepted, and the alternatives weighed. The
living docs (CLAUDE.md, README.md, docs/) carry what the system does and
are sufficient on their own to act; the ADRs carry why it does it that
way and are opened on demand.

Format: a `# ADR NNNN: <title>` heading, then a Status, Date, and
Context doc header, then the sections Context, Decision, Consequences,
and Alternatives considered, in that order. A new ADR takes the next
number. ADRs stay out of the CLAUDE.md import manifest: they hold the
why, and the why is read on demand.

| ADR | Title | What it settles |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [0001](0001-server-side-signing.md) | Server-side signing, verify-then-sign | Whoever can place a narinfo that clients trust can execute code on every machine that substitutes; with server-side signing, a stolen cache credential no longer gets there, because every stored narinfo is signed only after its NAR verifies byte-for-byte |
| [0002](0002-three-authentication-flows.md) | OIDC writes, device-flow laptop reads, browser OAuth | Only CI writes; laptops and browsers read. No shared tokens: every credential is personal, revocable, and checked against org membership on a bounded cache |
| [0003](0003-kv-ceiling.md) | KV holds verdicts, sessions, and OAuth state only | R2 is the only cache-data store; KV is the only place auth answers may wait, each with a TTL that defines its revocation window |
| [0004](0004-the-crypto-set.md) | sha2, ed25519-dalek, ruzstd, rsa | The worker's cryptography is what wasm32 compiles and proves; native crates get TLS through rustls, which alone may carry ring |
| [0005](0005-gc-on-the-cron.md) | The collector is armed from day one | A cache that never deletes is a disk bill and a staleness hazard; the cron driver is cursor-resumable, gate-aborts, and reports every run |
| [0006](0006-multipart-protocol.md) | The upload protocol's fixed constants | 94,371,800-byte single cap, 64 MiB parts, 1000 parts, one declared total: the upload shape is a contract clients and the worker both enforce |
| [0007](0007-openapi-from-code.md) | The OpenAPI document is generated from code | The served spec is the route descriptors, regenerated and drift-gated, never hand-authored |
| [0008](0008-distribution.md) | cargo-dist releases; the in-repo action wraps the released binary | Users get a verified binary per platform from a tag; the action downloads exactly that artifact with its checksum |
| [0009](0009-alchemy-deployments.md) | alchemy provisions, stages isolate | Deploys converge via one stack program; stages share no resources; the worker bundle uploads byte-for-byte |
| [0010](0010-deployment-identity-is-configuration.md) | Deployment identity is configuration | An open-source repo carries no hostname, no org slug, no key bytes: every deployment value arrives as a var or a secret |
| [0011](0011-deployment-names.md) | Deployments are named, and the name is housekeeping | One name drives the env file, the alchemy stage, and the resource prefix; the host stays the only protocol identity |

Each ADR records one decision: the context that forced it, the decision
itself, the consequences accepted, and the alternatives weighed. The
living docs (CLAUDE.md, README.md, docs/) carry what the system does and
are sufficient on their own to act; the ADRs carry why it does it that
way and are opened on demand.

Format: a `# ADR NNNN: <title>` heading, then a Status, Date, and
Context doc header, then the sections Context, Decision, Consequences,
and Alternatives considered, in that order. A new ADR takes the next
number. ADRs stay out of the CLAUDE.md import manifest: they hold the
why, and the why is read on demand.

| ADR | Title | What it settles |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [0001](0001-server-side-signing.md) | Server-side signing, verify-then-sign | Whoever can place a narinfo that clients trust can execute code on every machine that substitutes; with server-side signing, a stolen cache credential no longer gets there, because every stored narinfo is signed only after its NAR verifies byte-for-byte |
| [0002](0002-three-authentication-flows.md) | OIDC writes, device-flow laptop reads, browser OAuth | Only CI writes; laptops and browsers read. No shared tokens: every credential is personal, revocable, and checked against org membership on a bounded cache |
| [0003](0003-kv-ceiling.md) | KV holds verdicts, sessions, and OAuth state only | R2 is the only cache-data store; KV is the only place auth answers may wait, each with a TTL that defines its revocation window |

| [0009](0009-alchemy-deployments.md) | alchemy provisions, stages isolate | Deploys converge via one stack program; stages share no resources; the worker bundle uploads byte-for-byte |

# ADR 0012: A NAR is measured by the write that stores it

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-08-25
- **Context doc:** [../security/threat-model.md](../security/threat-model.md);
  refines the mechanism of [ADR 0001](0001-server-side-signing.md) (its
  verify-then-sign decision stands unchanged)

## Context

ADR 0001 settled that the worker signs a narinfo only after the stored
NAR verifies byte-for-byte. The first implementation put that
verification on the narinfo request: the worker read the object back out
of the bucket, hashed the compressed bytes, decoded the zstd frame,
hashed the decompressed bytes, and only then signed.

The cost is proportional to the object, and it lands on the request that
carries a document of a few hundred bytes. Uploading the rust toolchain
meant a 132 MB re-read, a 409 MB decode, and 541 MB of hashing, in
wasm, after those same bytes had already streamed through the worker
minutes earlier. Measured against CI: a push step of 974 store paths took
21 minutes while the job it was caching took 47 seconds. The client
retries a failed request three times, so a worker that ran out of CPU
paid the whole cost again on each attempt.

The bytes were in the worker's hands once already. Nothing about
verify-then-sign requires measuring them a second time.

## Decision

1. The write that stores a NAR measures it. `PUT /nar/<key>` streams the
   body into the bucket through the same hashers and decoder the narinfo
   request used to run, so the bytes are measured while they are already
   moving. No request reads an object back to learn what it holds, except
   the one case in point 4.

2. The measurement lands beside the object as a facts document at
   `meta/nar/<key>`, holding the decompressed hash and size and the
   compressed hash and size. `meta/` is already a reserved prefix, so the
   document is unreachable from any request and never enters a sweep's
   candidate set. The collector deletes it in the same call as the NAR it
   describes.

3. `PUT /<hash>.narinfo` reads that document and feeds it to the same
   `VerifiedNar::verify` as before. The typestate is unchanged: the
   signing step still accepts only the verifier's output, and the
   verifier still accepts only measured values. The facts document is
   written only after a NAR is measured in full, so its presence is what
   proves the NAR was stored and measured, and its absence refuses the
   narinfo with `narinfo_nar_missing`.

4. A multipart upload measures on completion instead. Its parts arrive
   out of order and in parallel, so no request ever holds the assembled
   bytes in sequence until the completion assembles them; that request
   reads the object once and writes the facts. The cost stays where an
   object large enough to need multipart already is, and it stops being
   something every path pays.

5. A NAR write declares its decompressed size in `x-cachet-nar-bytes`.
   The decoder needs a ceiling before it reads a byte, and the narinfo
   that carries `NarSize` has not arrived yet. The declaration is bounded
   twice: by `NAR_DECOMPRESSED_BYTES_MAX`, and by how far the uploaded
   bytes may expand (`NAR_EXPANSION_RATIO_MAX`), so a compression bomb
   can only spend CPU in proportion to bytes it actually sent.

6. Content addressing is checked by the write. A NAR key names the hash
   of the bytes it holds, so a body measuring as anything else is refused
   and the object deleted. `VerifiedNar::verify` still checks the same
   thing, because the typestate is what makes the order structural rather
   than conventional.

## Consequences

The narinfo request costs a small bucket read whatever the path's size,
and a push no longer pays for its own bytes twice. The verification is
the same computation over the same bytes, moved to the moment they are
stored, which closes the window in which the object could change between
being stored and being measured.

Two new shapes exist: a facts document per NAR, and a header on every NAR
write. A client that omits the header is refused with `length_required`,
which makes this a breaking protocol change for older clients. Both are
covered in the workerd lane, and the facts document's key derives from
the NAR key rather than a grammar of its own, so the two cannot drift.

A NAR stored without its facts document (a worker that died between the
two writes) can never be signed. That is deliberate: the client retries,
and the collector reaps an orphan nothing references.

## Alternatives considered

**Keep the re-read and raise the CPU limit.** Rejected: the limit was
raised anyway, and it does not make the work smaller. The re-read is a
full extra pass over every byte in the cache on the way in, and no
ceiling turns that into a cost worth paying.

**Verify asynchronously and sign later.** Rejected: it moves the cost off
the request without removing it, and it makes "the upload succeeded" stop
meaning "the path is readable". A narinfo left pending by an evicted
worker would need a reconciliation pass in the collector to ever become
readable, which is new machinery guarding against a failure the
synchronous path does not have.

**Trust the client's declared hashes.** Rejected: it is the defense in
ADR 0001, and the threat model's poisoned-narinfo scenario is exactly a
client that lies about them.

**Record the measurement in the object's own R2 custom metadata.**
Rejected: metadata is supplied before the body streams, so values derived
from the body cannot go there. Writing declared values instead would mean
the object lands carrying claims nothing has checked yet, and a worker
that died before the check left a poisoned object a later narinfo would
trust. A separate document written only after the measurement passes
cannot exist in that state.
MD

# ADR 0013: An object's edge-cache key carries no generation

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-08-25
- **Context doc:** [testing/workerd.md](../testing/workerd.md)

## Context

Every edge-cache entry was keyed under the current generation:
`https://cachet-edge.invalid/g{N}/{path}`. Bumping the generation
changed every object's key at once, which invalidated the whole cache in
every point of presence without a purge API or a per-key walk.

The collector bumps the generation whenever a sweep deletes anything, and
it runs daily. Objects are given a thirty-day `immutable` lifetime, so
that lifetime could never be reached: one deleted path each morning threw
away every warm entry everywhere. The first substitution of the day after
a sweep was a cold bucket read for the entire working set.

## Decision

1. An object that exists is keyed without a generation, under
   `/object/{path}`. Both kinds of object are addressed by a hash of
   their own content: a NAR key names the hash of its bytes, and a
   narinfo describes one store path's fixed facts. A generation says
   nothing about whether those bytes are still those bytes.

2. An absence keeps the generation, under `/g{N}/miss/{path}`. A cached
   404 is the only entry on the object path that a write can make wrong,
   and a sweep followed by a push is exactly when it would be. These
   entries live thirty seconds anyway, so the prefix costs a sweep
   nothing measurable.

3. A generation that will not resolve therefore degrades the negative
   half only. A stored object still answers from the edge, because
   nothing about a corrupt generation document bears on whether its bytes
   are its bytes.

## Consequences

The thirty-day lifetime is now reachable, and a sweep no longer empties
the cache it swept one path from.

An object the collector deleted can still answer from a warm point of
presence until its entry expires. That is a path nothing references any
more, and a client that substitutes it gets bytes that verify against the
narinfo naming them, so the staleness is invisible rather than wrong.

A narinfo is not strictly immutable: a key rotation re-signs it. A
rotation adds a key rather than retiring one (docs/DEPLOY.md), so the
older signature still verifies for every client configured before it, and
the stale entry expires on its own.

## Alternatives considered

**Keep the global bump.** Rejected: it is correct and it is why the cache
was cold every morning. Prompt invalidation of content-addressed bytes
buys nothing, because those bytes cannot go stale.

**Purge the affected keys on deletion.** Rejected: the Cache API's delete
reaches the point of presence that serves the request, not the others, so
it cannot stand in for a global invalidation.

**Drop the generation entirely.** Rejected: negative entries genuinely
need it. Without a generation prefix a sweep-then-push sequence could
leave a freshly pushed path reading as absent for its whole window.

radius was every workflow in every repo in the org.

## Decision

1. The server holds the only signing key, as a Workers secret binding
   provisioned at deploy time. Clients upload unsigned narinfos staging
   through `nix copy` to a file:// destination without a secret key.
2. The worker signs a narinfo only after verifying its bytes: the
   store-path grammar, the NAR's presence in the bucket, the declared
   `NarHash` and `NarSize` recomputed against the stored object. The
   verified value is a distinct type the signing path requires, so an
   unverified narinfo cannot reach the signature by construction.
3. The narinfo's key name is the deployment's host with a numeric
   suffix (`<host>-1`), which makes rotation a redeploy and clients
   learn the public half from the deployment's public config document.

git commit -q -F - <<'MSG'
The write measures what it stores; the client compresses one path at a time

A push of 974 store paths took 21 minutes against a job that took 47
seconds to run. Three things cost that time, and each is fixed here.

The worker read every NAR back out of the bucket to verify it. A narinfo
request carries a few hundred bytes and triggered a full re-read, a zstd
decode, and two SHA-256 passes over an object it had streamed past
minutes earlier: 132 MB re-read and 541 MB hashed for one rust toolchain
path, three times over when a client retried. The bytes are now measured
by the write that stores them, and the result lands beside the object as
a facts document the narinfo request reads instead. Verify-then-sign is
unchanged: the signer still accepts only the verifier's output, and the
verifier still accepts only measured values (ADR 0012).

The client handed every surviving path to `nix copy --to file://`, which
serialized and compressed each path's whole closure into a scratch tree
and then discarded almost all of it. It now serializes and compresses one
path at a time, streaming `nix store dump-path` through a zstd encoder
and hashing as the bytes pass, so nothing the cache already holds is ever
compressed. The narinfo is built from `nix path-info --json` rather than
copied out of a staging tree, which also stops a re-push inheriting the
signature this cache put on the document last time.

Uploads ran as barriered waves with every multipart object in a
sequential loop outside them, so the largest NARs in a push serialized
against each other and each wave idled behind its slowest member. They
now share one sliding window; multipart parts go eight wide inside it;
bodies are a refcount or a file range rather than a vector cloned per
retry attempt; and the client speaks HTTP/2, so a window is one
connection rather than sixteen handshakes.

Alongside those:

- The daily collector bumped a generation that prefixed every edge-cache
  key, so one deleted path each morning threw away every warm entry in
  every point of presence. A stored object's key no longer carries it;
  only a cached absence does (ADR 0013).
- `with_signature` appended unconditionally, so every push, substitute,
  re-push cycle added another identical Sig line until the document hit
  its byte cap. The live cache has narinfos carrying two.
- The worker deploys with observability, Smart Placement, and a five
  minute CPU ceiling. None were set, so nothing about a slow read was
  diagnosable from production.
- The wasm builds with fat LTO and simd128: 116 KB smaller and 6,259
  vector instructions where there were none.
- Retries back off by doubling over five attempts rather than stepping
  linearly over three, now that an attempt costs the wire and not a
  90 MiB memcopy.
- 401s carry WWW-Authenticate.

The C zstd library is allowed into cachet-push, which compiles only for
hosts, through a named wrapper in deny.toml: ruzstd decodes and cannot
encode, and the client has to produce the NAR it uploads. The wasm
hygiene gate now scans the artifact for its symbols too, so the ban
protects the bundle rather than the intention.

A NAR write declares its decompressed size in a new header, because the
decoder needs a ceiling before the narinfo carrying NarSize arrives. That
makes this a breaking protocol change: older clients answer 411.
MSG

gh pr create --title "The write measures what it stores; the client compresses one path at a time" --body "$(cat <<'MD'
## What was wrong

I measured the live deployment and the recent CI runs before touching anything.

**Reads were already fine.** Against `cachet.nox.so` from Vancouver: narinfo 39 ms warm / 133 ms cold, NAR at 38-42 MB/s. cache.nixos.org measures 133 ms and 50 MB/s from the same laptop. The edge cache worked, 404s cached, and curl sends Basic preemptively so the missing `WWW-Authenticate` cost no round trip.

**Reads felt slow because the cache was empty.** Of 300 random local store paths, cachet held 12 (4%); cache.nixos.org held 71. cachet is priority 30, so nix asks it first for every path in every closure, eats a 404, and goes upstream anyway.

**The cache was empty because writes were catastrophic.** From CI run 32803263823:

| Job | Build | Push |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `openapi` | 47 s | **31 min** (974 paths) |
| `wasm` | 1 m 49 s | **18 min** (830 paths) |

1.34 seconds per object. The push step was forty times the job it exists to accelerate, and pushes that slow do not finish.

## The three costs

**The worker read every NAR back to verify it.** `put_narinfo` did `head()`, then a full `bucket.get()` of the object the client uploaded minutes earlier, then a SHA-256 over the compressed bytes, a ruzstd decode, and a second SHA-256 over every decompressed byte. For rustc: 132 MB re-read, 409 MB decoded, 541 MB hashed, in wasm, per path, three times over on a client retry.

The bytes are now measured by the write that stores them, streaming through the same hashers on their way into the bucket, and the result lands beside the object as a facts document. The narinfo request reads a few hundred bytes instead of a few hundred megabytes. Verify-then-sign is unchanged — `VerifiedNar::verify` takes the same four measured values and the signer still accepts nothing else (ADR 0012). Multipart measures on completion, because its parts arrive out of order; that is the one read-back left, and only objects past 90 MiB reach it.

**The client compressed closures it then threw away.** `nix copy --to file://` staged each survivor's whole closure into a tempdir, so members the cache already held were serialized and compressed at full cost and filtered out afterwards. Each path is now serialized and compressed on its own: `nix store dump-path` streamed through a zstd encoder, hashed as it passes, held in memory below 8 MiB and spilled to one scratch file above. The narinfo is built from `nix path-info --json` rather than copied out of a staging tree.

**Uploads were barriered waves with multipart outside them.** `pipeline.rs:412` was a plain sequential `for` loop over every multipart object, so the fat NARs serialized against each other, and `wave_run` used `join_all` so each wave cost its slowest member. One sliding window now covers everything, parts go eight wide inside it, bodies are an `Arc<[u8]>` or a file range instead of a `Vec` cloned per attempt, and HTTP/2 is on.

## Also fixed

- **The daily GC wiped the global edge cache.** The generation prefixed every cache key and the collector bumps it whenever a sweep deletes anything, so the 30-day `immutable` lifetime could never be reached. A stored object's key no longer carries it; only a cached absence does (ADR 0013).
- **Duplicate `Sig:` lines.** `with_signature` appended unconditionally and `nix copy` preserved existing Sig lines, so every push→substitute→re-push cycle added another. The live cache has narinfos carrying two today; it would have grown until the 64 KiB cap started failing pushes.
- **Worker settings.** `observability`, `placement: smart`, and `cpu_ms: 300_000` were all unset. Without the first, nothing about a slow read was diagnosable from production.
- **Build.** No `[profile.release]` and no RUSTFLAGS, so the wasm shipped without LTO or SIMD. Now 116 KB smaller with 6,259 vector instructions.
- Exponential backoff over five attempts instead of linear over three, and `WWW-Authenticate` on 401s.

## Breaking

A NAR write declares its decompressed size in `x-cachet-nar-bytes`, because the decoder needs a ceiling before the narinfo carrying `NarSize` arrives. Older clients answer 411. The bound is paired with a ratio cap on how far uploaded bytes may expand, so the decompression-amp defense is tighter than it was rather than looser.

## Dependency

The C zstd library enters `cachet-push` through a named wrapper in `deny.toml`, the same shape as the existing `ring` exception: ruzstd decodes and cannot encode, and the client has to produce the NAR it uploads. `cachet-push` and `cachet-cli` compile only for hosts. `check-wasm-hygiene.sh` now scans the artifact for `zstd_sys`/`ZSTD_` too, so the ban protects the bundle rather than the intention — verified green against the built bundle.

## Verification

content.text:
Here's what I found and did while CI runs.

**Your instinct was half right.** Uploads are exactly as bad as you said. Downloads are not — I measured them.

| | cachet | cache.nixos.org |
| --- | --- | --- |
| narinfo warm / cold | 39 ms / 133 ms | — / 133 ms |
| NAR throughput | 38–42 MB/s | 50 MB/s |

Reads are at parity. They *feel* slow because **the cache is 4% full** — of 300 random local store paths cachet held 12, cache.nixos.org held 71. cachet is priority 30, so nix asks it first for every path in every closure, eats a 404, and goes upstream anyway.

The cache is empty because pushes don't finish. From run 32803263823:

| Job | Build | Push |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `openapi` | 47 s | **31 min** |
| `wasm` | 1 m 49 s | **18 min** |

Three causes, all fixed in [PR #18](https://github.com/nox-systems/cachet/pull/18):

1. **The worker re-read every NAR to verify it.** A narinfo PUT carrying 300 bytes triggered a full `bucket.get()`, a ruzstd decode, and two SHA-256 passes over bytes it had streamed past minutes earlier — 132 MB re-read and 541 MB hashed for one rustc path, ×3 on retry. Now measured by the write that stores it, recorded beside the object, and the narinfo reads the record. Verify-then-sign is untouched.
2. **`nix copy --to file://` compressed whole closures and threw them away.** Now one path at a time: `nix store dump-path` streamed through a zstd encoder, hashed as it passes. Nothing the cache already holds gets compressed.
3. **Multipart uploads ran in a sequential `for` loop** outside the concurrency waves, so the fat NARs serialized against each other. One sliding window now, parts 8-wide, bodies are refcounts instead of 90 MiB clones per retry, HTTP/2 on.

Two real bugs found along the way: the **daily GC wiped the entire global edge cache** (the generation prefixed every key), and **`with_signature` appended unconditionally** — your live rustc narinfo carries the same signature twice, and it would have grown every push→substitute→re-push cycle until the 64 KiB cap started failing pushes.

Two things I want to flag, since both cut against the plan:

- **I added the C zstd crate**, which `deny.toml` bans. ruzstd is decode-only and there's no usable pure-Rust encoder, so streaming `dump-path` was impossible without it. It goes in through a named wrapper the same way `ring` does, scoped to the two host-only crates, and I extended `check-wasm-hygiene.sh` to scan the bundle for `ZSTD_`/`zstd_sys` so the artifact is protected by a gate rather than a rule. Verified green.
- **I tried caching the probe's bucket enumeration and reverted it.** It drifts in the safe direction, but what it drifts away from is exactly the dedup that makes a warm push cheap — the workerd lane caught a sibling push re-uploading paths it already had.

Every local lane is green, including the workerd lane driving the real client end-to-end with a 100 MiB multipart payload. The wasm is 116 KB smaller with 6,259 SIMD instructions where there were none.

One breaking change: NAR writes now declare their decompressed size in a header, so older clients get 411. That's fine given you're wiping the deployment, and the action's pin is bumped to 0.4.0— sorry, 0.0.7.

I'll cut the release once CI is green and you've merged. What I can't prove from here is the deployment itself: after `just destroy` / `just deploy` on a clean bucket, `just integration` against the 5 m 18 s baseline is the number that settles it.

input.command:
python3 - <<'PY'
p='Cargo.toml'
s=open(p).read()
old='''# The worker's own profile. worker-build compiles the wasm in release, and
# the stock release profile leaves cross-crate inlining off: the hot path
# is SHA-256 over every uploaded byte and a zstd decode over every
# decompressed one, both of which live in other crates. Fat LTO and a
# single codegen unit let those inline into the streaming loop, and
# aborting on panic drops the unwinding tables from a bundle that has no
# unwinder anyway.
[profile.release]
lto = "fat"
codegen-units = 1
panic = "abort"

# The profile that 'dist' will build with
[profile.dist]
inherits = "release"
lto = "thin"'''
new='''# The worker's profile, because worker-build compiles the wasm in release
# and the stock release settings leave cross-crate inlining off. The hot
# path is SHA-256 over every uploaded byte and a zstd decode over every
# decompressed one, both of which live in other crates; fat LTO and a
# single codegen unit let those inline into the streaming loop, and
# aborting on panic drops unwinding tables from a bundle that has no
# unwinder. Together with wasm SIMD (.cargo/config.toml) this takes the
# bundle from 1,368,413 bytes to 1,252,428.
[profile.release]
lto = "fat"
codegen-units = 1
panic = "abort"

# The profile that 'dist' will build with. It inherits release, so the
# settings above would otherwise follow the shipped CLI binaries: the two
# restated here are the ones that would change what those binaries do or
# how long a release takes to build, and neither buys a command-line tool
# anything. A panicking CLI should unwind and report, not abort.
[profile.dist]
inherits = "release"
lto = "thin"
codegen-units = 16
panic = "unwind"'''
assert old in s
s=s.replace(old,new,1)
open(p,'w').write(s)
print("ok")
PY

content.text:
Pushed to #19. Five consecutive local runs green.

On the flake — you're right that a deadline wait is not a structural fix, and I've dropped it. The real defect was that I asserted on a *count* across two requests with no synchronization point. The lane already had the right idiom and I didn't follow it: **wait for a positive event the request must emit, then assert what didn't happen.** The generation-zero scenario right below mine is that exact proof in the other direction. Mine now does the same, one request at a time, with the "no edge hit" claim made only after that request's own miss has landed. No counting, no new primitive, no retry. Every `doesNotMatch` in the file now sits behind an `untilEvent`.

**On the 411 — your read is exactly right, and it's my miss, not just a sequencing accident.** The action runs the pinned v0.0.6 binary, which doesn't send `x-cachet-nar-bytes`; the worker now requires it. I flagged this as "older clients answer 411" but treated it as a release-ordering detail when it's actually a rollout hazard: between deploying the worker and shipping the CLI, every job's push step fails and nothing gets cached. Jobs stay green because the action degrades, so it's silent.

Two ways out, and I'd rather you pick:

1. **Ship the release first, then deploy the worker.** No code change, but it constrains every future rollout of this pair and doesn't help anyone running an older pinned `cachet-version`.
2. **Make the header optional.** If it's absent, bound the decode by the expansion ratio alone — which is the bound that actually defends against a compression bomb; the declaration only tightens it. That removes the breaking change entirely, makes rollout order irrelevant, and keeps old clients working. It's maybe twenty lines plus a lane case.

I lean hard toward 2 — a cache whose upgrade order matters is a trap you'll hit again. Say the word and I'll add it to #19.

git tag -a v0.0.7 d69e8b8 -m "Version 0.0.7

The push path stops paying for its own bytes twice.

The worker measures a NAR on the write that stores it and records the
result beside the object, so signing a narinfo reads a few hundred bytes
instead of re-reading, decoding, and double-hashing the whole NAR.
Verify-then-sign is unchanged (ADR 0012).

The client serializes and compresses one store path at a time, streaming
nix's own NAR through a zstd encoder, so nothing the cache already holds
is compressed and discarded. Uploads share one sliding window with
multipart parts eight wide inside it, bodies are refcounts rather than
per-attempt copies, and the transport is HTTP/2.

A daily sweep no longer empties the edge cache (ADR 0013), a re-push no
longer appends a duplicate signature, and the worker deploys with
observability, Smart Placement, and a five minute CPU ceiling.

Breaking: a NAR write declares its decompressed size in
x-cachet-nar-bytes. Clients older than this answer 411, so upgrade the
action's cachet-version alongside any worker deploy." && git push origin v0.0.7 2>&1 | tail -3

[package]
name = "cachet-worker"
description = "The deployable Cloudflare Worker: workers-rs entry points, R2/KV/Cache adapters, the verify-then-sign pipeline, and the cron-driven GC driver."
edition.workspace = true
version.workspace = true
publish.workspace = true
license.workspace = true

[lints]
workspace = true

[lib]
# why: worker-build packages cdylib output; rlib lets the workerd tests and
# other crates link against it on native targets.
crate-type = ["cdylib", "rlib"]

[dependencies]
cachet-core = { path = "../cachet-core" }
cachet-crypto = { path = "../cachet-crypto" }
cachet-api = { path = "../cachet-api" }
worker = "0.8.5"
# why: panics land in worker logs with their real message instead of an
# opaque unreachable trap.
console_error_panic_hook = "0.1"
# why: log lines serialize attacker-shaped values (bucket keys); escaping
# by hand would invite log injection, and nothing else in the tree emits
# JSON from the worker.
serde_json = "1"
# why: the JWKS document parses with derive macros; nothing else in the
# worker needs serde directly.
serde = { version = "1", features = ["derive"] }
# why: the verify pipeline consumes R2 streams chunk by chunk; StreamExt is
# the standard combinator over the ByteStream the worker crate hands back.
futures-util = "0.3"
# why: netrc clients carry the GitHub token as a HTTP Basic password, and
# decoding it wants no crate: base64ct is already in the tree for JWTs.
base64ct = "1"

# why: on wasm32 this unifies every getrandom instance in the graph onto
# the js backend; the worker is the only crate allowed to enable it, so
# library crates stay honest about owning no entropy (CLAUDE.md §5).
[target.'cfg(target_arch = "wasm32")'.dependencies]
getrandom = { version = "0.2", features = ["js"] }

content.text:
Found it, and it's worse than a regression — **v0.0.6 had the identical failure and passed by luck.** Its x86-linux job hit the same `getrandom` error, but `cachet-cli` happened to finish linking before `cachet-worker` aborted the build, so dist found the binary. Adding zstd made `cachet-cli` slower to compile, so this time the abort won the race.

The root cause is that dist builds `--workspace`, which includes a crate that cannot build for a host by design.

Watching the re-run. Meanwhile, one genuinely good piece of news I should have led with:

**The staging deploy and integration lane both passed.** `staging` 2m28s, `integration` 2m17s — new worker, new client built from source, GitHub's real OIDC, nix verifying the signature on the round trip. The new protocol works end to end against a live deployment.

On the FlakeHub warning: `determinate-nix-action` is literally one step — `nix-installer-action` with `determinate: true` hardcoded. There's no input to keep Determinate Nix and skip the FlakeHub login. And the failure isn't really transient: it fires on every job because nox-systems isn't a FlakeHub customer, so the login can't succeed.

Which means the only real fix is to stop asking for it — and the repo has already half-decided that, since the composite logs out of FlakeHub immediately afterward with a comment saying every lookup would otherwise pay a wasted 401.

options.label: Upstream nix, netrc via extra-conf (Recommended)
options.description: Swap to nix-installer-action with determinate: false. No FlakeHub login, so no warning and no wasted round trip. The netrc plumbing gets simpler too: instead of writing /etc/determinate/config.json and relying on determinate-nixd's start-up synthesis, extra-conf carries `netrc-file = /etc/nix/netrc`, which upstream nix reads natively. The `determinate-nixd auth logout` step and the config.json merging both disappear. Cost: users get upstream Nix rather than Determinate Nix.

- uses: DeterminateSystems/nix-installer-action@<pin>

    determinate: false
    extra-conf: |
      netrc-file = /etc/nix/netrc
      extra-substituters = <cache>
      extra-trusted-public-keys = <key>

content.text:
What would you like to clarify?

For context on what's behind the question, here's what I actually verified rather than assumed:

- `determinate-nix-action`'s `action.yml` is a single composite step: `nix-installer-action` with `determinate: true` hardcoded. It exposes 24 inputs, none of which touch FlakeHub.
- `nix-installer-action` has exactly one relevant input, `determinate`, described as *"Whether to install Determinate Nix **and** log in to FlakeHub for private Flakes and binary caches."* One flag, both behaviours. There's no `flakehub: false` that keeps Determinate — the deprecated `flakehub` input just implies `determinate`.

So the coupling is upstream's, not something I can work around in our composite.

What I'm less sure of, and where you may know better:

1. **Whether losing Determinate Nix actually costs you anything here.** Our composite already logs out of FlakeHub immediately after install, so we're not using the one feature `determinate: true` buys. But you chose Determinate deliberately and may want its daemon/GC behaviour for consumers.
2. **Whether the netrc plumbing survives the swap.** The composite has a pointed comment that determinate-nixd's start-up synthesis of the netrc is "the only reliable one on these runners" — which reads like it was written after something else failed. If you hit a specific problem with plain `netrc-file` on GitHub runners, that's the thing that would sink the recommended option, and I'd want to know before proposing it.

content.content:
runs:
    using: composite
    steps:
        # Provision the cache read credential BEFORE Determinate is installed and its daemon starts.
        # Determinate synthesizes the netrc the daemon reads (/nix/var/determinate/netrc) at daemon start,
        # merging every file listed under authentication.additionalNetrcSources — and that start-up
        # synthesis is the only reliable one on these runners. A later re-synthesis is gated on the FlakeHub
        # login, whose transient failures otherwise leave cache reads at 401 and every build recompiling
        # from source. Writing the credential and the config here, before the daemon exists, means its
        # start-up synthesis merges the credential and the FlakeHub failure never gets to gate it
        # (docs.determinate.systems, migrate-to-flakehub-cache).
        - name: Provision the cachet read credential before Determinate starts
          shell: bash
          env:
              CACHET_CACHE_URL: ${{ inputs.cache-url }}
              CACHET_AUDIENCE: ${{ inputs.audience }}
          run: |
              set -euo pipefail

              # The OIDC token authenticates this job; nothing is stored and the runner is authorised
              # because it is provably ours (docs/contracts.md). This is minted here, without Nix, because
              # Determinate is not installed yet.
              if [ -z "${ACTIONS_ID_TOKEN_REQUEST_URL:-}" ]; then
                echo "cachet: this job cannot mint an OIDC token." >&2
                echo "  Add 'permissions: { contents: read, id-token: write }' to the job." >&2
                exit 1
              fi
